The annual rainfall was extracted from the Climate Hazards group Infrared.
Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) dataset.
Starting from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-two.
Rainfall averages were extracted per state (three).
The estimated cases for each state.
Were calculated as a function of the modeled incidence estimates and the projected.
Population for that state.
As described in the World malaria report twenty twenty-two (four).
Population estimates used in this report are based on projections by state of the two thousand six.
Nigeria national census.
The World malaria report twenty twenty-two that is based on UN national population projections.
Affecting the overall estimates of cases.
Estimated cases averted over the period two thousand nine–twenty twenty-one were computed by comparing.
Estimates for each year since two thousand nine with the malaria case incidence rates from two thousand nine.
Adjusting for population growth.
The year two thousand nine was selected as the baseline (or.
Counterfactual in the absence of interventions) considering that this was the year.
When first mass insecticide-treated nets (ITN) campaigns were implemented.
Data on distribution of ITNs and SMC were provided by the NMEP.
Malaria prevalence.
Treatment seeking.
Diagnosis and ITN coverage indicators were extracted from the.
Household survey reports.
Health facility level monthly IPTp data were extracted.
The number of first and second doses of IPTp and the total number.
Of first antenatal care visits were aggregated to calculate the national and state.
Level coverage of IPTpone and IPTptwo per year.
Coverage was calculated by dividing.
The number of IPTpone or IPTptwo doses by the total number of first antenatal care visits.
Reports that had missing data for one or more of the data elements were excluded.
From the analysis.
Data were checked for consistencies and outliers.
When appropriate.
To improve data quality.

Discussion Ghana adopted a phased approach in the malaria vaccine introduction with an initial schedule of six, seven, nine, and twenty-four months [twenty-two, twenty-three].
The study assessed the impact of the RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria episodes among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The trend of vaccine uptake reflects the pathway of the introduction process in the region and the country at large.

The study is not without limitations.
Further, only data from facilities reporting in DHIMS-two were used for the study.
Data from private health facilities, community pharmacies and alternative practitioners were unavailable.
Furthermore, the impact of the vaccine on severe malaria was not assessed due to inadequate data.
Lastly, attribution rates for IRS, and LSM for the study areas, respectively, could not be estimated due to incomplete data.
The application of attribution rates from other studies could impact reliability of the results.
Conclusion The study assessed the impact of routine use of RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The vaccine reduced episodes of uncomplicated malaria by thirty-three percent.
Although the malaria incidence averted decreased marginally over time, the impact on uncomplicated malaria remained significant.

Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax are the most prevalent, and P. falciparum is the most virulent species [one–four].
The co-existence of these two species makes malaria control more complicated [five–seven].
Most of these cases were coming from countries in the World Health Organization (WHO) African Region [eight].
The WHO and UN (United Nations) Habitat indicated that by twenty fifty nearly seven out of ten people globally will live in cities and urban settings.
Unplanned growth of urbanization and the spread of the invasive malaria vector Anopheles stephensi make malaria control in urban areas difficult.
The spread of this vector into Africa further complicates the already complex malaria situation.
This vector appears to swiftly acclimate to its surroundings and thrives in manmade water containers in urban settings.
Moreover, the vector has also exhibited resistance to several classes of insecticides.
Urbanization has significant epidemiological, entomological, parasitological, and behavioural implications on malaria risks.
The global patterns of disease and mortality, including malaria, will change due to a shift in the human population from rural to urban areas.
Besides, the epidemiology of urban malaria since the spread of a new mosquito vector species, An.
Stephensi, in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopia, is not well studied [twelve].
For urban malaria control strategies to be successful, it must be directed at the urban areas where infections are occurring.
If infections are contracted in cities, similar actions must be targeted differently.
Because of this, effective urban malaria control depends on accurate clinical and epidemiologic data [eighteen].
Therefore, this study identified urbanassociated socioenvironmental determinants of urban malaria in Eastern Ethiopia.

Knowledge To assess the participants’ knowledge on malaria, its control and prevention, twelve knowledge related questions were used.
An overall knowledge score was calculated by adding all scores for each respondent for all knowledge related questions.
Attitude Attitude was assessed using thirteen attitude related Likert scale questions.
An overall attitude score was calculated by using principal component analysis and finally dichotomized as poor and good.
Data collection tool and procedure Data were collected by ODK software with the tool developed from different relevant and related literatures.
The questionnaire was translated to both Afan Oromo and Amharic languages and back translated to English to check for consistency.
Both thick and thin blood smears were prepared on a clean, labeled microscopic slide for each selected study participant.
Finally, the slides were stained with ten percent Giemsa for ten min, air dried, and examined microscopically by an experienced laboratory technologist.
The slides were considered negative if no parasite was seen after examining one hundred high power fields.
To ensure the quality of data, pretest was done among five percent of the sample size at Laga Hare Health center in Dire Dawa city.

Two vaccines are approved and starting to be deployed, bringing additional protection for children up to thirty-six months.
However, the impact of these currently available tools is somewhat limited on various fronts.
Vaccines exhibit partial efficacy, are relatively costly, and not accessible in all settings.
Also, the emergence of resistance against chemopreventive medicines is concerning.
This TPP describes the ideal product attributes, while acknowledging potential trade-offs that may be needed.
Critically, it considers the target populations most at risk; primarily infants, children, and pregnant women.
New medicines should show acceptable safety and tolerability, with high and long protective efficacy.
Formulations and costs need to support operational adherence, access, and effectiveness.
Next generation long-acting oral and injectable drugs are likely to constitute the backbone of malaria prevention.
Therefore, the perspectives of front-line experts in malaria prevention, researchers, and those involved in drug development are captured in the TPP.
This inclusive approach aims at concentrating efforts and aligning responses across the community to develop new and transformative medicines.

Indeed, two hundred forty-nine million cases and six hundred eight thousand deaths were reported in twenty twenty-two, with over ninety-four percent of deaths occurring in sub-Saharan Africa [one].
Malaria prevention is targeted at populations most at risk of severe malaria living in moderate-to-high transmission areas (Fig. two).
Additionally, intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy (IPTp) is recommended in the second and third trimester [two].
PMC, IPTsc, and IPTp are reliant on sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) and SMC uses the combination of SP and amodiaquine (SPAQ).
However, the effectiveness of these interventions is at risk from the potential spread of high-level SP resistance [four– seven].
For travellers, atovaquone-proguanil is used for chemoprophylaxis but is not widely used within Africa.
Overview of current malaria prevention interventions.
Understanding how and where this combination can be effectively implemented at scale will be an important research question for the future.
The progress in protecting pregnant women has been inadequate [twenty-two].
Neither of the current malaria vaccines is approved for use in adults.
Chemoprevention with SP is contraindicated in pregnant women living with HIV and in all women in the first trimester of pregnancy.
Consequently, SMC among five–ten-year-old children is being implemented in some countries [twenty-five, twenty-six].
A revised target product profile (TPP) outlining both the minimal acceptable and ideal profiles of chemopreventive drug combinations is proposed.
The overarching objective of the TPP is to propose a road map to guide and boost the development of a future generation of chemopreventive options.
However, there are specific key gaps in provision and critical unmet needs for each group.
The most widely adopted chemopreventive strategy in Africa is SMC.
Although PMC and IPTsc have been piloted in several countries, widespread implementation has not followed.
Barriers to implementation include practical issues such as the need to crush tablets, and poor integration with childhood health services [thirty-one, thirty-two].
The intervention is highly cost-effective, reducing infection by fourfold in clinical trial settings in children under five years of age [thirty-three, thirty-four].
However, where SMC has been deployed, shifts in the disease burden to older age groups have been detected [twenty-five, twenty-six, thirty-five, thirty-six].
Consequently, MMV supports the expansion of SMC to children aged five–ten years, as currently being implemented in some countries [twenty-five, twenty-six].
For many years, SMC was not deployed in the seasonal zones of Eastern Africa, though this is now being tested [thirty-seven–thirty-nine].
There is also the risk that widespread deployment of SMC will drive further resistance selection to SP or to amodiaquine [forty-one–forty-three].
Another key limitation is the need to administer amodiaquine for three days per month [forty-four, forty-five].
The adoption of chemoprevention in pregnancy has been limited.
IPTp with at least three courses of SP is recommended after week thirteen of pregnancy to protect women and reduce adverse outcomes [two, forty-six].
Despite the extremely low cost of IPTp and the single dose monthly schedule, adherence and coverage remains poor.
This is partially explained by concerns about the anti-malarial efficacy of SP [fifty-one, fifty-two].
Another important limitation is the lack of options for women living with HIV and the unmet need for all women in theirEl Gaaloul et al.

To address the need for infrequent dosing, the concept of long-acting injectables with small molecules also requires exploration [fifty-four].
Additionally, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) currently in development for malaria show encouraging findings [fifty-six–fifty-eight].
Rationale for revising the target product profile (TPP) The TPP is designed to set the expectations for the next generation of medicines.
It is, therefore, timely to consolidate the outcome of various discussions on malaria prevention in a revised chemoprevention TPP.
It is also important to consider to what extent these tools can be implemented in an integrated and complementary manner for maximal impact.

However, as malaria elimination programmes progress, heterogeneity in transmission is inevitable.
Malaria epidemics associated with heavy rains and floods occurring in usually dry areas have also been reported [seventy].
The second approach is the recombine individual molecules from existing treatment combinations to make new products [sixty-two].
Although the safety of the individual medicines is well known, there is the potential for emergent adverse events with the new combination [seventy-one].
Thus, potential drug–drug interactions, safety, tolerability, and efficacy of the recombination must be evaluated.
From both a development and regulatory perspective, recombination is more demanding than repurposing [sixty-two].
The third strategy is the most challenging, but with greatest potential for developing products that address the limitations of current interventions.
It requires molecule optimization in the discovery phase to produce pharmacological duration of protection of at least a month.
Target populations The minimum essential target populations include those most at risk of malaria (Fig.
Thus, the TPP considers several options (OR statements) so that a drug which has value in one population is not discarded.
Children under ten years of age living in malaria-endemic regions are particularly vulnerable to malaria infection and its associated complications.
Malnourished children and those with sickle cell disease represent high-risk subgroups and should ideally be considered in product development.
To address this need, compounds with no teratogenic signals in animal studies should be prioritized for development.

Study design A retrospective observational analysis was conducted to evaluate the epidemiological and entomological impact of PBO ITNs.

Vector surveillance Two entomological outcome indicators analysed were human biting rate and indoor resting density.
Human biting rate was defined as the number of An.
Mosquitoes collected by U.
Indoor resting density was defined as the number of An.
Collected indoors by pyrethrum spray catch (PSC) per room per day.
Vector surveillance was conducted at six sampling sites in three LGAs, two sites per LGA (Supplemental Table four).
Indoor-resting mosquitoes were collected using PSCs in thirty-two houses per site per month.
Teams followed standard operating procedures for CDC LT and PSC collections [twenty-two, twenty-three].
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays were carried out on approximately ten percent of the mosquitoes collected to identify members of the An.
The extracted DNA was amplified using the An.
Gambiae species-specific multiplex PCR [twenty-four, twenty-five].
Ward and health facility were included as random effects, with health facility nested within ward.
The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) method was used to determine which combination of lagged climate variables was the best fit.
The three climate covariates were scaled to have a mean of zero and standard deviation of one.

Finally, the overall higher malaria burden in Ebonyi during the pre-distribution period may have provided an opportunity to observe a greater decline.
To date, this is one of the first studies in Nigeria to evaluate the epidemiological and entomological impacts of a newer type of ITN.
The positive epidemiological impact of PBO ITNs is similar to findings from previous assessments.
The trends observed in both Ebonyi and Cross River are also similar to those reported between the twenty eighteen DHS [seventeen] and the twenty twenty-one MIS [eighteen].
In Cross River, malaria prevalence by RDT increased by fifty-four percent and malaria prevalence by microscopy increased by twenty-one percent.

Briefly, the SDSS consists of a centralized database server, a geographic grid-based household coding system, and a form-based data collection system.
The grid-based system is constructed around a onexone km areas grid, forty-seven such areas correspond to Malabo and one hundred ninety-three to the rural periphery (Fig.
MDC data to estimate LLIN crop The twenty fifteen and twenty eighteen MDC took place between October twenty fourteen and July twenty fifteen and between February and November twenty eighteen.
These campaigns targeted every household on the island, but could not reach those found closed or where residents would not accept the intervention.
The twenty twenty-one MDC in the periphery had the same configuration as the previous campaigns and was conducted between mid June and mid July.
Data from MDC were used to obtain the number of LLINs distributed per household.
MIS data to estimate actual net crop and LLIN indicators Annual MIS data between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-two were used.
Individual-level data were linked to the corresponding household, which in turn was linked to the SDSS geographical grid [eight, ten].
Surveyed individuals were asked whether they slept under a LLIN the night before.
Formally, estimates of use should be based on de facto household members.
Those who slept in the house.
However, this information was captured from twenty nineteen Nt = Ng + Ns onwards only.
For comparability across years, LLIN use was estimated based on de jure members.
All household members.
MIS also enquire about the number of LLINs available at the household, or LLINs declared and abbreviated Nd.
Whenever possible, surveyors corroborated their presence by observing LLINs within the household.
In addition, for each individual net, specific information is recorded, including the source.
LLIN indicators were calculated as recommended by the World Health Organization and as illustrated in Fig. two.
Population access was calculated according to individual access to LLINs within the household, assuming each net serves two people.
Indicators were based on Nd and LLIN use the previous night from the MIS.
Standard survey data analysis techniques were applied to account for the sampling design, as follows.
A two-level stratified cluster design was declared using primary sampling units (PSUs) and households as clusters.
For each PSU, the sampling probability was set to one.
In addition, a finite population correction was performed to account for the fact that all PSUs were sampled.
A target of eighty percent coverage was used as the reference for evaluating indicators against universal coverage.

Finally, there are cultural and socioeconomic factors that determine some people are more prone to adhering to malaria interventions than others [nineteen].
Adherence is one critical driver for the success of any intervention and this also varies across areas of Bioko Island.
MDCs are a resource intensive strategy.
This is particularly the case in densely populated urban areas, such as Malabo.
To provide context, the island-wide twenty fifteen and twenty eighteen MDC took around six months to implement with a workforce of about ninety people.
In contrast, the twenty twenty-one MDC, which was limited to the periphery, took one month and required the effort of only sixteen workers.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
The rationale behind this shift was to optimise resources while guaranteeing LLIN access to the people who use them.
The significant increase in twenty twenty-two to a fifth of households sourcing their nets from these facilities was encouraging.
However, U
Efforts should focus on reinforcing SBCC to raise population awareness of where LLINs are available when they are needed.
The question of what is the optimal distribution strategy for the periphery remains unanswered.
This approach would rely on an assessment of housing characteristics and other metrics such as socioeconomic status [seventeen].
Continuous monitoring of LLIN indicators will shed light on how best to tailor the intervention.
Guaranteeing population access is the first step towards closing the net use gap [two].
Many programmes continue to rely on MDCs every two to three years to provide their populations with high LLIN coverage.
Furthermore, LLIN indicators frequently drop steeply relatively soon after distribution compromising use, as observed on Bioko [twenty-seven, twenty-eight].
The strategy in Malabo prioritizes giving nets to those members of the population who need them and who would use them.
Moreover, sustaining the fixed distribution points saved the programme considerable resources relative to conducting MDC.

Conclusions Laboratory experiment on the susceptibility of An.
Gambiae to five, ten and fifteen mg/ml (+)-UA when administered as oral sugar bait has first been demonstrated by this study.
Mortality for both males and females is higher in the first four h of exposure and continues up to seventy-two h.

Folami S. and Marcus J.
Proinflammatory mediators are thought to play a central role in its pathogenesis.
Correlations between these biomarker and plasma lactate and Plasmodium falciparum histidine‑rich protein two (PfHRPtwo) levels were evaluated.
Results Of one hundred six screened patients with falciparum malaria, fifty-six were classified as having severe malaria with a mortality rate of twenty-nine percent.
Nine (sixteen percent) patients developed clinical pulmonary oedema after admission.
Plasma levels of the biomark‑ ers of interest were higher in patients compared to healthy controls.
IL‑six, IL‑eight, TNF, sRAGE, and CCsixteen levels correlated well with plasma PfHRPtwo levels (rs = zero point four).
Furthermore, IL‑six and IL‑eight levels correlated well with plasma lactate levels (rs = zero point two).
None of the biomarkers of interest had predictive capacity for development of clinical pulmonary oedema.
Conclusions IL‑six, IL‑eight, TNF, sRAGE, SP‑D, CCsixteen and KL‑six cannot be used in predicting clinical pulmonary oedema in severe malaria patients.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Pulmonary oedema is a well-known and severe complication carrying high mortality in patients with severe malaria [two].
The pathogenesis of pulmonary oedema in severe malaria is not fully elucidated.
Fluid overload could exacerbate pulmonary oedema; therefore, dry fluid management is required in patients with severe malaria [five, six].
Intravenous fluid administration, however, is not a primary cause of the lung complications.
Predicting pulmonary oedema could be valuable in managing severe malaria by facilitating prompt respiratory support.
In this exploratory study, therefore, the predictive capacity of various plasma biomarkers for clinical pulmonary oedema was assessed.
Written informed consent was obtained from patients or attending relatives before enrollment.
This study was registered at clinicaltrials.
Gov (identifier NCTone million, nine hundred thirty-six thousand, seven hundred sixty-six).
Patients and clinical assessment Consecutive patients admitted with falciparum malaria in the rainy seasons during twenty thirteen–twenty fourteen were included.
Eligibility criteria for enrollment was presence of asexual Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia confirmed by peripheral blood microscopy.
The exclusion criteria was absence of consent.
The diagnosis of falciparum malaria was confirmed with microscopic examination of smears of peripheral blood specimens by Field stain.
Uncomplicated malaria was defined as asexual P. falciparum slide positivity without severity criteria.
Healthy individuals with no known acute or chronic illnesses were recruited locally as a comparison group for assessment of biomarker measurement.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was defined by the new global definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome [thirteen].
A detailed medical history was recorded, and a physical examination was performed in all patients.
The FiOtwo values in lowflow oxygen-delivery system were predicted by oxygen flow rates described in Supplement one [fifteen].
Fluid intake and urine output were recorded every six h.
Antimalarial treatment was with intravenous artesunate, and standard supportive care was given according to WHO guidelines [sixteen].
The availability of mechanical ventilation and renal replacement therapy was limited.
Laboratory procedures On admission, venous blood samples were taken for full blood count and routine biochemistry analysis.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Arterial blood gas analysis was not always performed since the procedure was not a routine clinical practice in the study sites.
Concentrations of PfHRPtwo were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Cellabs), as described before [seventeen].
Plasma samples for biomarkers were shipped to and analysed in batches in the Amsterdam University Medical Centers, location AMC, the Netherlands.
Endpoint The endpoint was the development of clinical pulmonary oedema after admission.
Statistical analysis A formal sample-size calculation was not performed.
The number of consecutive patients in the rainy season served as the sample size.
Levels of biomarkers of interest in malaria patients and in healthy volunteers were compared.

The proinflammatory biomarkers were increased in proportion to disease severity, while no such trend was observed for the lung injury biomarkers.
This study had several strengths of a prospective nature with a clearly defined study population of high severity, at high risk of pulmonary oedema.
Patients with clinical pulmonary oedema on admission were excluded from the analysis for biomarker predictivity.
A large set of biomarkers that have shown to have associations with outcome in previous studies was used.
The batchwise measurements was advantageous method to prevent laboratory variations.
Critically ill patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
In line with previous investigations, biomarkers for inflammation were rather correlated with prognostic indicators of plasma PfHRPtwo.
Indeed, a correlation between IL-six and plasma lactate was found in a previous study [twenty].
Important in this context is that there is no evidence that a higher parasite biomass is more likely to cause pulmonary oedema.
Interestingly, biomarkers for lung injury did not correlate with known prognostic predictors and were also not predictive of pulmonary oedema.
RAGE is a member of the immunoglobulin super-family and a multiligand transmembrane receptor expressed mainly in the alveolar type-one cells.
SRAGE, the form lacking the transmembrane domain, might be a candidate predictor for the diagnosis of ARDS [seven, eight, twenty-one].
The concentrations of sRAGE were correlated with parasite biomass but did not predict clinical pulmonary oedema from the ROC curves.
In patients with severe malaria, pulmonary oedema often develops after initiation of antimalarial drugs.
The median time from hospitalization to the onset of pulmonary oedema in this study was thirty h.
In this study, sampling was performed on admission promptly after participant consent was obtained.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Tunji B., Kunle Rotimione, Azuka Iwegbuone, Olusola Oresanya, Julianna Smith, Kolawole Maxwellone, and Tarekegn A.
In Nigeria, ITNs have been periodically distributed since two thousand seven through campaigns.
Campaign activities and assets are typically tracked using either a paper-based or digital system.
In twenty seventeen, a digital approach was introduced in Ondo state for tracking attendance at training sessions as part of the ITN campaign.
This article presents lessons and experiences from the twenty twenty-one ITN distribution campaign in Ondo state, Nigeria.
ITNs were delivered through a single-phase door-to-door distribution strategy.
Results The campaign distributed two million, nine hundred sixty-five thousand, one hundred twenty-five ITNs covering one million, fifty-seven thousand, five hundred seventy-seven households across Ondo state.
The digital application was beneficial for monitoring the quality of implementation and tracking assets and staff to ensure safety.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
In twenty seventeen, a digital platform was piloted in Kwara state to track the distribution of ITNs.
The same year Ondo state used a digital platform during the ITN distribution campaign to track attendance at training sessions [seven].
The emergence of a novel coronavirus in twenty nineteen and the subsequent COVID-nineteen pandemic impacted the twenty twenty-one ITN campaign.
To ensure the campaign could go ahead safely, several adaptations were made to the campaign, in particular to the distribution strategy.
During the twenty twenty-one campaign a single-phase door-to-door distribution strategy was used to reduce inter-household mixing.
This paper details the lessons from digitising the ITN distribution campaign and the adaptations made to the distribution strategy.
Methods Context Ondo state is situated in Southwest Nigeria.
Ondo state is made up of eighteen Local Government Areas (LGAs) and two hundred three political wards.
In twenty twenty-one, the state population was projected to be approximately five.
The twenty eighteen Demographic and Health Survey found that Ondo state had a high malaria prevalence while access to ITNs was insufficient [nine].
To determine the number of ITNs required, the total population was divided by one.
eight and a ten percent buffer was added as recommended by national and international guidelines [ten, eleven].
LGA technical assistants then travelled to their respective LGAs to orientate the ward teams, carry out data collection and conduct advocacy visits.
Demand creation Demand creation activities took place to raise awareness of, and support for, the ITN distribution campaign.
Orientation sessions included information about COVID-nineteen, including the symptomsAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Location of Ondo state, NigeriaAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Protocols to prevent COVID-nineteen transmission were introduced and monitored during all trainings.
The adaptations included ensuring there was adequate space at training venues for participants to maintain a distance of at least one.
Mobilization and distribution Typically, ITN campaigns use a double-phase fixed-point distribution strategy.
The first phase involves a mobilization visit to households.
During the visit health education sessions are also carried out to provide information on malaria and how to use and care for nets.
The second phase is where representatives of households travel to a fixed location with their net cards to collect the ITNs they are eligible for.
In comparison, this campaign adopted a single-phase door-todoor distribution strategy.
This strategy involved a single visit to households where mobilization, enumeration and ITN distribution were carried out simultaneously.
Where there were an uneven number of household members the number was rounded up.
This information was delivered in the local language and covered malaria, COVID-nineteen and how to use and care for ITNs.
Post‑distribution survey A household survey was conducted four months after the campaign in fifty-two sampled wards to monitor household ownership of ITNs.
A second digital platform, SurveyCTO, was used for in-process and end-process monitoring.
The set up included checking whether devices worked, charging batteries and managing set up including geolocation settings.
The training covered use of the Android devices and mobile application and who to contact with issues.
Hands-on practical simulations and role plays were used to promote effective learning.
This also allowed the LGA coordinators to meet the teams they would be supervising in advance to build rapport.
Cluster supervisors, who were responsible for supervising a collection of two–three wards, were also trained on the cash and asset transfer strategy.
A cash and asset transfer strategy is used to monitor the movement of financial and material assets.
During all training sessions COVID-nineteen transmission prevention protocols were followed.
After training sessions, the devices were distributed to the mobilization and distribution teams.
Tracking attendance All training sessions conducted at state, LGA and ward level were tracked using the mobile application.
The process of logging attendance was monitored by the ICTfourD team and data were checked daily to ensure completeness.
These ID cards allowed them to log the registration and issuance of ITNs to households and the collection and return of ITNs at the distribution hub.
The data were also reviewed by the state team to confirm the targeted number of ITNs had been distributed.
Training and Technology Assistants were also available at their respective ward clusters to provide additional supportive supervision.
In-process monitoring was also carried out by the state and LGA teams, LGA Technical Assistants and Campaign Implementation Teams using SurveyCTO.
Each monitor randomly sampled ten households and three distribution hubs daily for the duration of the activity in any LGA or ward they visited.
Data analysis The data collected during the mobilization and distribution phase were monitored and analysed in real-time by the ICTfourD team.
This enabled the team to monitor the success of the campaign by calculating the cumulative ITNs distributed and obtain the distribution rate.
The undistributed ITNs returned by the mobilization and distribution team were also verified and recorded.
Daily review meetings were held at LG/A and state level to review the data collected and activities carried out.
These meetings helped to identify and resolve problems quickly and improved the quality of implementation.
Outcomes Macro‑quantification and procurement The macro-quantification estimated the population of Ondo state to be five million, three hundred sixty-one thousand three in twenty twenty-one (Table one).
The numberAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
sixty-two thousand, two hundred thirty-four ITNs more than the number required after the micro-quantification).
The mobilization phase recorded twenty fifty-five fewer households and an increase of three hundred twenty-five thousand, five hundred sixty-seven in the population, compared to the microplanning results.
The increase in population may be due to the microplanning using an estimate of five people per household.
During the distribution two hundred seventy-two thousand, six hundred forty-one fewer ITNs were delivered compared to the number predicted by the microplanning.
The difference between the number procured and the number distributed was three hundred thirty-four thousand, eight hundred seventy-five, equivalent to ten point one percent of the total ITNs procured.
one percent of the total ITNs procured.
The percentage of households with at least one ITN increased from twenty-three point eight percent.
eight percent, and the de facto population with access to an ITN within their households increased from sixteen point five percent.
The percentage of households with at least one campaign net for every two people was fifty-three point five percent.
Most households (seventy-nine percent) received between one and four campaign nets.
Approximately four percent of households received five or more nets.
Out of the sampled households, seventeen percent did not receive campaign nets.
In addition, a few other benefits were observed as a result of adopting a single-phase door-to-door approach.
First, adopting this approach meant that enumeration, mobilisation and distribution was conducted simultaneously.
Therefore, there was no need to distribute net cards to households in advance of the distribution.
This was an advantage as it reduced the amount of paper required for the campaign and the cost of production and distribution of the cards.
Challenges Several challenges were also observed due to the adaptations made to the training schedule and mobilisation and distribution strategy.
First, during the training, additional materials were developed to teach staff about COVID-nineteen symptoms and prevention.
The agenda for training sessions was already full, and the extra information added pressure to this schedule.
This led to insufficient time to focus on the main deliverables, which could have compromised the quality of delivery.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
For this reason, there was a greater reliance on the micro-quantification for calculating the number of ITNs needed in each area.
In addition, if no one was home at the time of the visit the distribution teams had to re-visit at another time.
In some cases, distribution teams did not re-visit and these households were missed.
The additional time needed to distribute nets had a knock-on effect and reduced the amount of time for health talks.
Finally, households were notified that the distributors would deliver ITNs to their door.
This caused confusion as households had waited at home for ITNs to be delivered and in some cases, households did not receive or collect ITNs.
Lessons from digitizing the campaign Benefits Digitising the ITN campaign had several benefits.
Collecting data using digital devices meant teams did not have to carry paper forms around with them which can be heavy.
In addition, collecting data digitally allowed supervisors to carry out in-process monitoring of the campaign in real-time.
Supervisors were able to track the location of each device to ensure teams were carrying out the campaign in their assigned areas.
The devices also recorded information such as the number of distributions carried out by the team and the length of time between distributions (Fig. two).
Data points demonstrating the geolocation of ITN distribution.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
First, when logging distribution data in the RedRose app was when distributors did not have the location settings set to a precise enough value.
In addition, there were challenges when logging the collection and return of ITNs at distribution hubs.
Ideally all distributors would have scanned their ID badge to record the number collected or returned.
This error resulted in discrepancies between predicted stock and actual stock of ITNs at the distribution.
Map showing mobilization and distribution with each mobilizers informationAdeniyi et al.
The macroplanning for this campaign used data from a census conducted fifteen years prior [eight].
High-quality precise data is essential to procure accurate resources.
Improvements in data quality could lead to savings in purchasing commodities and transportation costs while avoiding under-estimations.
In addition, poor data quality has implications for the allocation of resources.
Some of the information gathered for the microplanning missed settlements or had to be updated.
In addition, automated systems could be used to notify programme planners when adjustments are needed.
The single-phase door-to-door approach was more convenient for households, removing the necessity to travel to a fixed point, at a specified time.
In addition, the removal of net cards has the potential to reduce the gap between allocation and collection and improve ITN coverage.
More investigation is needed to understand if the adapted approach improved household ITN coverage compared to the fixed-point approach.
An additional consideration is the impact of the doorto-door approach on the quality of health education delivered to households.
The information collected during this campaign will also help to inform and plan future ITN distributions.
Digital tools are a helpful way to improve the planning and delivery of ITN campaigns efficiently.
However, the use of these tools requires additional training for mobilisation and distribution teams to ensure these tools are used correctly.

Conclusion The prevalence of dissemination bias and outcome reporting bias in interventional malaria research is significant.
Addressing these biases necessitates enhancing the quality of both registration and publication processes.
Implementing measures to ensure timely research dissemination within WHO-recommended timeframes is crucial for enhancing transparency.
The findings from this study support the WHO’s recommended timelines for disseminating results broadly.

Unplanned growth of urbanization and the spread of the invasive malaria vector Anopheles stephensi make malaria control in urban areas difficult.
The spread of this vector into Africa further complicates the already complex malaria situation.
This vector appears to swiftly acclimate to its surroundings and thrives in manmade water containers in urban settings.
Moreover, the vector has also exhibited resistance to several classes of insecticides.
Urbanization has significant epidemiological, entomological, parasitological, and behavioural implications on malaria risks.

Data collection tool and procedure Data were collected by ODK software with the tool developed from different relevant and related literatures.
The questionnaire was translated to both Afan Oromo and Amharic languages and back translated to English to check for consistency.
Both thick and thin blood smears were prepared on a clean, labeled microscopic slide for each selected study participant.
Finally, the slides were stained with ten percent Giemsa for ten min, air dried, and examined microscopically by an experienced laboratory technologist.
The slides were considered negative if no parasite was seen after examining one hundred high power fields.
To ensure the quality of data, pretest was done among five percent of the sample size at Laga Hare Health center in Dire Dawa city.

The region occupies a land mass of eight thousand, eight hundred forty-two square kilometres and constitute two point seven  percent of the total landmass.
seven percent of the total landmass of Ghana [eleven].
It has fifteen administrative districts and one hundred one sub-districts.
The projected population from the twenty twenty-one census was one million, three hundred eighteen thousand, five hundred twenty-three, with children twelve–fifty-nine months constituting sixteen percent [eleven].
The land is relatively flat, with a few hills to the East and Southeast.
Most of the eastern and western parts of the region lie within the basins of the Volta River and its tributaries.
Upper East has a tropical wet and dry or savanna climate with yearly temperature of thirty-one point six  percent higher than Nigeria's average.
six percent higher than Ghana’s averages [eleven].
It has one rainfall season that begins in May, peaks in August, and lasts until September and typically receives about forty-four point two.

Discussion Ghana adopted a phased approach in the malaria vaccine introduction with an initial schedule of six, seven, nine, and twenty-four months [twenty-two, twenty-three].
The study assessed the impact of the RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria episodes among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The trend of vaccine uptake reflects the pathway of the introduction process in the region and the country at large.
three Trend of RTS,S malaria vaccination coverage, Upper East Region, Ghana; twenty twenty–twenty twenty-twoAdjei et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
From the study, there was thirty-three percent (ninety-five percent CI twenty-nine–thirty-six) reduction in uncomplicated malaria episodes in the implementing area.
The observation highlights the need to strengthen the use of other malaria control measures in malaria vaccine Fig.
four Malaria incidence and incidence ratios, MVIP impact study, Upper East Region, Ghana; twenty twenty–twenty twenty-twoAdjei et al.
The study is not without limitations.
Further, only data from facilities reporting in DHIMS-two were used for the study.
Furthermore, the impact of the vaccine on severe malaria was not assessed due to inadequate data.
Lastly, attribution rates for IRS, and LSM for the study areas, respectively, could not be estimated due to incomplete data.
The application of attribution rates from other studies could impact reliability of the results.
Conclusion The study assessed the impact of routine use of RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The vaccine reduced episodes of uncomplicated malaria by thirty-three percent.
Although the malaria incidence averted decreased marginally over time, the impact on uncomplicated malaria remained significant.

The intervention is highly cost-effective, reducing infection by fourfold in clinical trial settings in children under five years of age [thirty-three, thirty-four].
However, where SMC has been deployed, shifts in the disease burden to older age groups have been detected [twenty-five, twenty-six, thirty-five, thirty-six].
Consequently, MMV supports the expansion of SMC to children aged five–ten years, as currently being implemented in some countries [twenty-five, twenty-six].
For many years, SMC was not deployed in the seasonal zones of Eastern Africa, though this is now being tested [thirty-seven–thirty-nine].
There is also the risk that widespread deployment of SMC will drive further resistance selection to SP or to amodiaquine [forty-one–forty-three].
Another key limitation is the need to administer amodiaquine for three days per month [forty-four, forty-five].
The adoption of chemoprevention in pregnancy has been limited.
IPTp with at least three courses of SP is recommended after week thirteen of pregnancy to protect women and reduce adverse outcomes [two, forty-six].
Despite the extremely low cost of IPTp and the single dose monthly schedule, adherence and coverage remains poor.
This is partially explained by concerns about the anti-malarial efficacy of SP [fifty-one, fifty-two].
Another important limitation is the lack of options for women living with HIV and the unmet need for all women in theirEl Gaaloul et al.

To address the need for infrequent dosing, the concept of long-acting injectables with small molecules also requires exploration [fifty-four].
Additionally, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) currently in development for malaria show encouraging findings [fifty-six–fifty-eight].
Rationale for revising the target product profile (TPP) The TPP is designed to set the expectations for the next generation of medicines.
It is, therefore, timely to consolidate the outcome of various discussions on malaria prevention in a revised chemoprevention TPP.
It is also important to consider to what extent these tools can be implemented in an integrated and complementary manner for maximal impact.

However, as malaria elimination programmes progress, heterogeneity in transmission is inevitable.
Malaria epidemics associated with heavy rains and floods occurring in usually dry areas have also been reported [seventy].
The second approach is the recombine individual molecules from existing treatment combinations to make new products [sixty-two].
Although the safety of the individual medicines is well known, there is the potential for emergent adverse events with the new combination [seventy-one].
Thus, potential drug–drug interactions, safety, tolerability, and efficacy of the recombination must be evaluated.
Again, there is a risk for resistance selection where chemoprevention drugs and treatment drugs contain the same active ingredients.
From both a development and regulatory perspective, recombination is more demanding than repurposing [sixty-two].
The third strategy is the most challenging, but with greatest potential for developing products that address the limitations of current interventions.
It requires molecule optimization in the discovery phase to produce pharmacological duration of protection of at least a month.

Thus, the TPP considers several options (OR statements) so that a drug which has value in one population is not discarded.
Children under ten years of age living in malaria-endemic regions are particularly vulnerable to malaria infection and its associated complications.
Malnourished children and those with sickle cell disease represent high-risk subgroups and should ideally be considered in product development.
To address this need, compounds with no teratogenic signals in animal studies should be prioritized for development.

Plasmodium vivax has become the most prevalent parasite in areas where malaria transmission is declining [seventy-three].
There also remains the threat of primate malaria, such as Plasmodium knowlesi, whose long-term impact on malaria elimination remains unclear.
The ability to target multiple lifecycle stages is an advantage but not an absolute requirement.
Atovaquone-proguanil brought the additional benefit of activity against hepatic schizonts.
For this revised TPP, a minimal essential profile would be two compounds with activity against parasite blood stages.
However, compounds with activity against liver schizonts or even those with transmission blocking would bring additional value to the product [three].

From a public health perspective, chemoprevention in pregnancy should also improve maternal anaemia and birth outcomes, such as low birthweight.
However, it is important to underline that any regimen which can confer a malaria-free pregnancy for the mother is a significant breakthrough.
Therefore, maternal malaria is recommended here as the primary endpoint for minimal acceptable chemopreventive efficacy.
Finally, the drugs used for malaria chemoprevention should preferably not be used for case management in the same regions.
This would reduce drug selection pressure for each drug class with the aim of retaining antimalarial efficacy for longer.
Preventive medication is administered to healthy or asymptomatic individuals who are not at immediate risk of poor outcome.
In terms of ideal characteristics, there are opportunities to improve safety, tolerability, and acceptability over the standard-of-care.
For example, developing medicines with the potential for use throughout all trimesters of pregnancy would be a significant advance.
Pregnancy testing is not always accepted, particularly for young unmarried women, and may not be available to identify women in their first trimester.
For IPTp, current SP dosing is a single administration of three large tablets with five hundred twenty-five mg active ingredient.
Food effect and drug–drug interactions Ideally, oral chemoprevention should have no requirements for food intake.
However, food restrictions after oral drug administration may be acceptable if they are limited in duration.
Without a full clinical assessment of the risk–benefit, it is difficult to set a numerical boundary on the fasting duration and degree of food effect.
A food effect study with a high-fat meal should be conducted for all orally administered drugs [eighty-eight].
However, the effect of a local diet should ideally be considered as it may be more pertinent to the habits in malaria-endemic regions.

The target population may be exposed to concomitant medications like antibiotics, HIV and TB drugs, and oral contraception.
Therefore, manageable drug–drug interactions with dose adjustments should be expected as a minimum.
These restrictions are particularly important for the long-acting injectable medicines.

In addition, a three-day dosing regimen would also be acceptable in cases where no other options are available or recommended.
Oral products should preferably be formulated as fixed dose combinations.
However, co-packaged partner drug formulations may be acceptable if fixed dose combination is not feasible.
Formulations need to have high acceptability by the target population.
Palatability and convenience are key considerations for chemoprevention to avoid sub-optimal dosing.
For example, dispersible tablets can be given more easily to children and should be taste-masked and/or sweetened.
Similarly, the pill burden needs to be acceptable, for example, in pregnant women who may be nauseous.
In addition, injections on two separate sites was deemed acceptable.
The injection volume and needle size were of less importance, if they remained within the currently accepted standards (injection volumes from zero point five mL).

Vector surveillance was conducted at six sampling sites in three LGAs, two sites per LGA (Supplemental Table four).
Indoor-resting mosquitoes were collected using PSCs in thirty-two houses per site per month.
Teams followed standard operating procedures for CDC LT and PSC collections [twenty-two, twenty-three].

The extracted DNA was amplified using the An.

Ward and health facility were included as random effects, with health facility nested within ward.

To date, this is one of the first studies in Nigeria to evaluate the epidemiological and entomological impacts of a newer type of ITN.
The positive epidemiological impact of PBO ITNs is similar to findings from previous assessments.
The trends observed in both Ebonyi and Cross River are also similar to those reported between the twenty eighteen DHS [seventeen] and the twenty twenty-one MIS [eighteen].
In Cross River, malaria prevalence by RDT increased by fifty-four percent and malaria prevalence by microscopy increased by twenty-one percent.

Briefly, the SDSS consists of a centralized database server, a geographic grid-based household coding system, and a form-based data collection system.
The grid-based system is constructed around a onexone km areas grid, forty-seven such areas correspond to Malabo and one hundred ninety-three to the rural periphery (Fig.
MDC data to estimate LLIN crop The twenty fifteen and twenty eighteen MDC took place between October twenty fourteen and July twenty fifteen and between February and November twenty eighteen.
These campaigns targeted every household on the island, but could not reach those found closed or where residents would not accept the intervention.
The twenty twenty-one MDC in the periphery had the same configuration as the previous campaigns and was conducted between mid June and mid July.
Data from MDC were used to obtain the number of LLINs distributed per household.
MIS data to estimate actual net crop and LLIN indicators Annual MIS data between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-two were used.
Individual-level data were linked to the corresponding household, which in turn was linked to the SDSS geographical grid [eight, ten].
Surveyed individuals were asked whether they slept under a LLIN the night before.
Formally, estimates of use should be based on de facto household members.
Those who slept in the house.
However, this information was captured from twenty nineteen Nt = Ng + Ns onwards only.
For comparability across years, LLIN use was estimated based on de jure members.
All household members.
MIS also enquire about the number of LLINs available at the household, or LLINs declared and abbreviated Nd.
Whenever possible, surveyors corroborated their presence by observing LLINs within the household.
In addition, for each individual net, specific information is recorded, including the source.
LLIN indicators were calculated as recommended by the World Health Organization and as illustrated in Fig. two.
Population access was calculated according to individual access to LLINs within the household, assuming each net serves two people.
Indicators were based on Nd and LLIN use the previous night from the MIS.
Standard survey data analysis techniques were applied to account for the sampling design, as follows.
A two-level stratified cluster design was declared using primary sampling units (PSUs) and households as clusters.
For each PSU, the sampling probability was set to one.
In addition, a finite population correction was performed to account for the fact that all PSUs were sampled.
A target of eighty percent coverage was used as the reference for evaluating indicators against universal coverage.

Finally, there are cultural and socioeconomic factors that determine some people are more prone to adhering to malaria interventions than others [nineteen].
Adherence is one critical driver for the success of any intervention and this also varies across areas of Bioko Island.
MDCs are a resource intensive strategy.
This is particularly the case in densely populated urban areas, such as Malabo.
To provide context, the island-wide twenty fifteen and twenty eighteen MDC took around six months to implement with a workforce of about ninety people.
In contrast, the twenty twenty-one MDC, which was limited to the periphery, took one month and required the effort of only sixteen workers.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
The rationale behind this shift was to optimise resources while guaranteeing LLIN access to the people who use them.
The significant increase in twenty twenty-two to a fifth of households sourcing their nets from these facilities was encouraging.
However, U
Efforts should focus on reinforcing SBCC to raise population awareness of where LLINs are available when they are needed.
The question of what is the optimal distribution strategy for the periphery remains unanswered.
This approach would rely on an assessment of housing characteristics and other metrics such as socioeconomic status [seventeen].
Continuous monitoring of LLIN indicators will shed light on how best to tailor the intervention.
Guaranteeing population access is the first step towards closing the net use gap [two].
Many programmes continue to rely on MDCs every two to three years to provide their populations with high LLIN coverage.
Furthermore, LLIN indicators frequently drop steeply relatively soon after distribution compromising use, as observed on Bioko [twenty-seven, twenty-eight].
The strategy in Malabo prioritizes giving nets to those members of the population who need them and who would use them.
Moreover, sustaining the fixed distribution points saved the programme considerable resources relative to conducting MDC.

Folami S. and Marcus J.
Proinflammatory mediators are thought to play a central role in its pathogenesis.
Correlations between these biomarker and plasma lactate and Plasmodium falciparum histidine‑rich protein two (PfHRPtwo) levels were evaluated.
Results Of one hundred six screened patients with falciparum malaria, fifty-six were classified as having severe malaria with a mortality rate of twenty-nine percent.
Nine (sixteen percent) patients developed clinical pulmonary oedema after admission.
Plasma levels of the biomark‑ ers of interest were higher in patients compared to healthy controls.
IL‑six, IL‑eight, TNF, sRAGE, and CCsixteen levels correlated well with plasma PfHRPtwo levels (rs = zero point four).
Furthermore, IL‑six and IL‑eight levels correlated well with plasma lactate levels (rs = zero point two).
None of the biomarkers of interest had predictive capacity for development of clinical pulmonary oedema.
Conclusions IL‑six, IL‑eight, TNF, sRAGE, SP‑D, CCsixteen and KL‑six cannot be used in predicting clinical pulmonary oedema in severe malaria patients.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Pulmonary oedema is a well-known and severe complication carrying high mortality in patients with severe malaria [two].
The pathogenesis of pulmonary oedema in severe malaria is not fully elucidated.
Fluid overload could exacerbate pulmonary oedema; therefore, dry fluid management is required in patients with severe malaria [five, six].
Intravenous fluid administration, however, is not a primary cause of the lung complications.
Predicting pulmonary oedema could be valuable in managing severe malaria by facilitating prompt respiratory support.
In this exploratory study, therefore, the predictive capacity of various plasma biomarkers for clinical pulmonary oedema was assessed.
Written informed consent was obtained from patients or attending relatives before enrollment.
This study was registered at clinicaltrials.
Gov (identifier NCTone million, nine hundred thirty-six thousand, seven hundred sixty-six).
Patients and clinical assessment Consecutive patients admitted with falciparum malaria in the rainy seasons during twenty thirteen–twenty fourteen were included.
Eligibility criteria for enrollment was presence of asexual Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia confirmed by peripheral blood microscopy.
The exclusion criteria was absence of consent.
The diagnosis of falciparum malaria was confirmed with microscopic examination of smears of peripheral blood specimens by Field stain.
Uncomplicated malaria was defined as asexual P. falciparum slide positivity without severity criteria.
Healthy individuals with no known acute or chronic illnesses were recruited locally as a comparison group for assessment of biomarker measurement.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was defined by the new global definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome [thirteen].
A detailed medical history was recorded, and a physical examination was performed in all patients.
The FiOtwo values in lowflow oxygen-delivery system were predicted by oxygen flow rates described in Supplement one [fifteen].
Fluid intake and urine output were recorded every six h.
Antimalarial treatment was with intravenous artesunate, and standard supportive care was given according to WHO guidelines [sixteen].
The availability of mechanical ventilation and renal replacement therapy was limited.
Laboratory procedures On admission, venous blood samples were taken for full blood count and routine biochemistry analysis.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Arterial blood gas analysis was not always performed since the procedure was not a routine clinical practice in the study sites.
Concentrations of PfHRPtwo were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Cellabs), as described before [seventeen].
Plasma samples for biomarkers were shipped to and analysed in batches in the Amsterdam University Medical Centers, location AMC, the Netherlands.
Endpoint The endpoint was the development of clinical pulmonary oedema after admission.
Statistical analysis A formal sample-size calculation was not performed.
The number of consecutive patients in the rainy season served as the sample size.
Levels of biomarkers of interest in malaria patients and in healthy volunteers were compared.

The proinflammatory biomarkers were increased in proportion to disease severity, while no such trend was observed for the lung injury biomarkers.
This study had several strengths of a prospective nature with a clearly defined study population of high severity, at high risk of pulmonary oedema.
Patients with clinical pulmonary oedema on admission were excluded from the analysis for biomarker predictivity.
A large set of biomarkers that have shown to have associations with outcome in previous studies was used.
The batchwise measurements was advantageous method to prevent laboratory variations.
Critically ill patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
In line with previous investigations, biomarkers for inflammation were rather correlated with prognostic indicators of plasma PfHRPtwo.
Indeed, a correlation between IL-six and plasma lactate was found in a previous study [twenty].
Important in this context is that there is no evidence that a higher parasite biomass is more likely to cause pulmonary oedema.
Interestingly, biomarkers for lung injury did not correlate with known prognostic predictors and were also not predictive of pulmonary oedema.
RAGE is a member of the immunoglobulin super-family and a multiligand transmembrane receptor expressed mainly in the alveolar type-one cells.
SRAGE, the form lacking the transmembrane domain, might be a candidate predictor for the diagnosis of ARDS [seven, eight, twenty-one].
The concentrations of sRAGE were correlated with parasite biomass but did not predict clinical pulmonary oedema from the ROC curves.
In patients with severe malaria, pulmonary oedema often develops after initiation of antimalarial drugs.
The median time from hospitalization to the onset of pulmonary oedema in this study was thirty h.
In this study, sampling was performed on admission promptly after participant consent was obtained.

Tunji B., Kunle Rotimione, Azuka Iwegbuone, Olusola Oresanya, Julianna Smith, Kolawole Maxwellone, and Tarekegn A.
In Nigeria, ITNs have been periodically distributed since two thousand seven through campaigns.
Campaign activities and assets are typically tracked using either a paper-based or digital system.
In twenty seventeen, a digital approach was introduced in Ondo state for tracking attendance at training sessions as part of the ITN campaign.
This article presents lessons and experiences from the twenty twenty-one ITN distribution campaign in Ondo state, Nigeria.
ITNs were delivered through a single-phase door-to-door distribution strategy.
Results The campaign distributed two million, nine hundred sixty-five thousand, one hundred twenty-five ITNs covering one million, fifty-seven thousand, five hundred seventy-seven households across Ondo state.
The digital application was beneficial for monitoring the quality of implementation and tracking assets and staff to ensure safety.
High-quality population data are needed to further improve the planning and implementation of ITN campaigns and other health interventions.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
In twenty seventeen, a digital platform was piloted in Kwara state to track the distribution of ITNs.
The same year Ondo state used a digital platform during the ITN distribution campaign to track attendance at training sessions [seven].
The emergence of a novel coronavirus in twenty nineteen and the subsequent COVID-nineteen pandemic impacted the twenty twenty-one ITN campaign.
To ensure the campaign could go ahead safely, several adaptations were made to the campaign, in particular to the distribution strategy.
During the twenty twenty-one campaign a single-phase door-to-door distribution strategy was used to reduce inter-household mixing.
This paper details the lessons from digitising the ITN distribution campaign and the adaptations made to the distribution strategy.
Methods Context Ondo state is situated in Southwest Nigeria.
Ondo state is made up of eighteen Local Government Areas (LGAs) and two hundred three political wards.
In twenty twenty-one, the state population was projected to be approximately five.
The twenty eighteen Demographic and Health Survey found that Ondo state had a high malaria prevalence while access to ITNs was insufficient [nine].
To determine the number of ITNs required, the total population was divided by one.
eight and a ten percent buffer was added as recommended by national and international guidelines [ten, eleven].
The resulting quantity was then rounded up to maximize the space available in shipping containers.
Micro‑quantification and transportation Micro-planning activities were concluded four months ahead of the campaign.
LGA technical assistants then travelled to their respective LGAs to orientate the ward teams, carry out data collection and conduct advocacy visits.
Demand creation Demand creation activities took place to raise awareness of, and support for, the ITN distribution campaign.
Orientation sessions included information about COVID-nineteen, including the symptomsAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Location of Ondo state, NigeriaAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
Protocols to prevent COVID-nineteen transmission were introduced and monitored during all trainings.
The adaptations included ensuring there was adequate space at training venues for participants to maintain a distance of at least one.
Mobilization and distribution Typically, ITN campaigns use a double-phase fixed-point distribution strategy.
The first phase involves a mobilization visit to households.
During the visit health education sessions are also carried out to provide information on malaria and how to use and care for nets.
The mobilization and enumeration activities are typically carried out one–two weeks before the ITN distribution.
The second phase is where representatives of households travel to a fixed location with their net cards to collect the ITNs they are eligible for.
In comparison, this campaign adopted a single-phase door-todoor distribution strategy.
This strategy involved a single visit to households where mobilization, enumeration and ITN distribution were carried out simultaneously.
Where there were an uneven number of household members the number was rounded up.
This information was delivered in the local language and covered malaria, COVID-nineteen and how to use and care for ITNs.
Post‑distribution survey A household survey was conducted four months after the campaign in fifty-two sampled wards to monitor household ownership of ITNs.
A second digital platform, SurveyCTO, was used for in-process and end-process monitoring.
The set up included checking whether devices worked, charging batteries and managing set up including geolocation settings.
The training covered use of the Android devices and mobile application and who to contact with issues.
Hands-on practical simulations and role plays were used to promote effective learning.
This also allowed the LGA coordinators to meet the teams they would be supervising in advance to build rapport.
Cluster supervisors, who were responsible for supervising a collection of two–three wards, were also trained on the cash and asset transfer strategy.
A cash and asset transfer strategy is used to monitor the movement of financial and material assets.
During all training sessions COVID-nineteen transmission prevention protocols were followed.
After training sessions, the devices were distributed to the mobilization and distribution teams.
Tracking attendance All training sessions conducted at state, LGA and ward level were tracked using the mobile application.
The process of logging attendance was monitored by the ICTfourD team and data were checked daily to ensure completeness.
These ID cards allowed them to log the registration and issuance of ITNs to households and the collection and return of ITNs at the distribution hub.
The data were also reviewed by the state team to confirm the targeted number of ITNs had been distributed.
Training and Technology Assistants were also available at their respective ward clusters to provide additional supportive supervision.
In-process monitoring was also carried out by the state and LGA teams, LGA Technical Assistants and Campaign Implementation Teams using SurveyCTO.
Each monitor randomly sampled ten households and three distribution hubs daily for the duration of the activity in any LGA or ward they visited.
Data analysis The data collected during the mobilization and distribution phase were monitored and analysed in real-time by the ICTfourD team.
This enabled the team to monitor the success of the campaign by calculating the cumulative ITNs distributed and obtain the distribution rate.
The undistributed ITNs returned by the mobilization and distribution team were also verified and recorded.
Daily review meetings were held at LG/A and state level to review the data collected and activities carried out.
These meetings helped to identify and resolve problems quickly and improved the quality of implementation.
Outcomes Macro‑quantification and procurement The macro-quantification estimated the population of Ondo state to be five million, three hundred sixty-one thousand three in twenty twenty-one (Table one).
The numberAdeniyi et al.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
sixty-two thousand, two hundred thirty-four ITNs more than the number required after the micro-quantification).
This required ITNs to be redistributed from one LGA or ward to another to ensure there was sufficient stock to cover the change in population.
The mobilization phase recorded twenty fifty-five fewer households and an increase of three hundred twenty-five thousand, five hundred sixty-seven in the population, compared to the microplanning results.
The increase in population may be due to the microplanning using an estimate of five people per household.
During the distribution two hundred seventy-two thousand, six hundred forty-one fewer ITNs were delivered compared to the number predicted by the microplanning.
The difference between the number procured and the number distributed was three hundred thirty-four thousand, eight hundred seventy-five, equivalent to ten point one percent of the total ITNs procured.
one percent of the total ITNs procured.
The percentage of households with at least one ITN increased from twenty-three point eight percent.
eight percent, and the de facto population with access to an ITN within their households increased from sixteen point five percent.
The percentage of households with at least one campaign net for every two people was fifty-three point five percent.
five percent overall (unpublished data).
The post-campaign survey also showed that the number of nets received by households ranged from zero to ten.
Most households (seventy-nine percent) received between one and four campaign nets.
Approximately four percent of households received five or more nets.
Out of the sampled households, seventeen percent did not receive campaign nets.
In addition, a few other benefits were observed as a result of adopting a single-phase door-to-door approach.
First, adopting this approach meant that enumeration, mobilisation and distribution was conducted simultaneously.
Therefore, there was no need to distribute net cards to households in advance of the distribution.
This was an advantage as it reduced the amount of paper required for the campaign and the cost of production and distribution of the cards.
Challenges Several challenges were also observed due to the adaptations made to the training schedule and mobilisation and distribution strategy.
First, during the training, additional materials were developed to teach staff about COVID-nineteen symptoms and prevention.
The agenda for training sessions was already full, and the extra information added pressure to this schedule.
This led to insufficient time to focus on the main deliverables, which could have compromised the quality of delivery.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
For this reason, there was a greater reliance on the micro-quantification for calculating the number of ITNs needed in each area.
In addition, if no one was home at the time of the visit the distribution teams had to re-visit at another time.
In some cases, distribution teams did not re-visit and these households were missed.
The additional time needed to distribute nets had a knock-on effect and reduced the amount of time for health talks.
Finally, households were notified that the distributors would deliver ITNs to their door.
This caused confusion as households had waited at home for ITNs to be delivered and in some cases, households did not receive or collect ITNs.
Lessons from digitizing the campaign Benefits Digitising the ITN campaign had several benefits.
Collecting data using digital devices meant teams did not have to carry paper forms around with them which can be heavy.
In addition, collecting data digitally allowed supervisors to carry out in-process monitoring of the campaign in real-time.
Supervisors were able to track the location of each device to ensure teams were carrying out the campaign in their assigned areas.
The devices also recorded information such as the number of distributions carried out by the team and the length of time between distributions (Fig. two).
Data points demonstrating the geolocation of ITN distribution.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
First, when logging distribution data in the RedRose app was when distributors did not have the location settings set to a precise enough value.
In addition, there were challenges when logging the collection and return of ITNs at distribution hubs.
Ideally all distributors would have scanned their ID badge to record the number collected or returned.
This error resulted in discrepancies between predicted stock and actual stock of ITNs at the distribution.
Map showing mobilization and distribution with each mobilizers informationAdeniyi et al.
Further study is needed to confirm whether this approach would be feasible, acceptable and beneficial.
The macroplanning for this campaign used data from a census conducted fifteen years prior [eight].
High-quality precise data is essential to procure accurate resources.
Improvements in data quality could lead to savings in purchasing commodities and transportation costs while avoiding under-estimations.
In addition, poor data quality has implications for the allocation of resources.
Some of the information gathered for the microplanning missed settlements or had to be updated.
In addition, automated systems could be used to notify programme planners when adjustments are needed.
The single-phase door-to-door approach was more convenient for households, removing the necessity to travel to a fixed point, at a specified time.
In addition, the removal of net cards has the potential to reduce the gap between allocation and collection and improve ITN coverage.
More investigation is needed to understand if the adapted approach improved household ITN coverage compared to the fixed-point approach.
An additional consideration is the impact of the doorto-door approach on the quality of health education delivered to households.
The information collected during this campaign will also help to inform and plan future ITN distributions.
Digital tools are a helpful way to improve the planning and delivery of ITN campaigns efficiently.
However, the use of these tools requires additional training for mobilisation and distribution teams to ensure these tools are used correctly.

We may have had malaria since we evolved from the apes.

The first concerted attack against malaria started in the nineteen fiftys.

State Department in charge of the health talks.

Everything should be done to them and for them.

They are doing tons of malaria research.
And they understand the economic challenge too.
Theyre focusing on very cheap, very easy-to-use tools.

The centerpiece of the current effort is the bed net.
Its treated with insecticides.
