Discussion Malaria transmission peaks during the rainy season, with  significant variations across different ecological zones in  the country [twenty-six].
Simi larly, malaria cases peaked in these months compared  to other months as shown in Table one.
Malaria RDT TPR  were almost similar between CUfive and persons ≥ five years  both in PHCs and secondary health facilities as seen in  this study.
Several studies have shown that malaria is more preva lent in rural areas compared to urban areas, hence often  described as a disease of the poor.
One study attributed  this difference to better living conditions and access to  healthcare facilities in urban areas [twenty-seven].
This study  also shows that in the two-year study period, test positivity  rate was highest in the rural LGAs and least in the semi urban LGAs.
The stratification lacked a clear distinc tion as factors that characterize very large urban settings  reducing malaria transmission intensity (e.
One Malaria RDT test positivity rate across primary health facilities from January twenty twenty-one–December twenty twenty-two Ayandipo et al.
Malaria Journal Page eight of twelve Fig.
Additionally, as this is an hospital-based study, the  incidence of malaria cannot be well elucidated.
These include inconsistent  data reporting, suboptimal use of diagnostic tools, and  gaps in healthcare worker training.
In this study, the average TPR was higher for RDT  (sixty-five percent) compared to microscopy (thirty-four percent).
This is similar to  what has been found in other studies [thirty-two].
Before the facility audits of RDT, a very high TPR  among febrile clients tested for malaria with RDT was  noted in the health facilities.
These figures, compared  to survey data, raise questions about the accuracy of  the routinely collected health facility data.
For instance,  data from Therapeutic Efficacy Study (TES) conducted  in Ibadan Oyo reported that the malaria incidence in  twenty twenty-one was forty-five.
Seven percent [thirty-four] compared to health facility test  positivity rates of seventy-one percent in the same year.
Field visits  often reveal inaccuracies in documentation and some times data falsification.
Malaria Journal provider’s cadre and previous training on other causes  of fever [thirty-five].
Some  studies have shown inflation of data or overreporting  of services provided, in addition to reclassification of  cases [thirty-five–thirty-seven].
This study showed improvement and a  reduction in the test positivity rate because of accurate  and improved data capture.
Prior to cassette archiv ing, this study revealed that the average reported TPR at  PHCs was seventy-seven percent, while it reduced to fifty-eight percent after archiving  commenced.
This is similar to the malaria TPR of fifty-five percent  reported in a twenty twenty-one hospital-based survey in Ibadan [eleven].
Malaria diagnosis using microscopy not only detects  Plasmodium species but also allows for speciation and  parasite density counting.
Training malaria micros copists significantly improves the accuracy of malaria  microscopy test results.
Following BMMT in Septem ber twenty twenty-one, the overall prevalence of malaria in this study  using microscopy was twenty-nine percent.
This study revealed a reduc tion in test positivity rates at the selected facilities after  the BMMT training.
Malaria Journal Page ten of twelve control efforts by reducing the number of false positive  test results.
This is particularly important in the context  of malaria elimination efforts, where accurate data is  critical for monitoring progress.
These measures would not only ensure the reliability of reported data  but also contribute to informed decision-making and  targeted interventions.
One limitation of this study is the  absence of comparative data from other states in Nigeria  where the interventions were not implemented.
This lack of comparison limits the ability to conclusively attribute  the observed improvements in TPR accuracy solely to the  interventions.
Conclusion The accuracy of reported data is another major concern  in the fight against malaria.
Factors contributing to data  inaccuracy include the reclassification of negative test  results as positive.
This practice not only skews malaria  prevalence statistics but also leads to the inappropriate  use of ACT, which can promote drug resistance.
The introduction of facility audits for RDTs has shown  promising results in improving data accuracy.
This study revealed a significant reduction in the test positivity rate  after the implementation of cassette archiving and audits.
Similar improve ments were noted in accuracy of reports from malaria  microscopy following the basic malaria microscopy  training.
Improving the accuracy of malaria diagnosis is criti cal for effective health service planning and achiev ing malaria control targets.
Continued investment in training, infrastructure, and  regular audits will help address the challenges faced in  malaria diagnosis.
Accurate data is essential for meas uring progress, making informed decisions, and ulti mately reducing the burden of malaria in Nigeria.
By addressing these challenges, Nigeria can make signifi cant strides towards better health outcomes and con trol of malaria.
The authors also appreciate all the  health workers in Oyo for always doing their best to report accurate data in a  timely manner.
The efforts and time taken by the reviewers  assigned to review this paper by the journal are also appreciated.

This study aimed to determine the prevalence and factors associated  with malaria and anaemia among children aged two–eighteen months in Osun State.
Methods A cross-sectional household malariometric study was conducted in eighty communities across eight Local Gov ernment areas (LGAs) in Osun State.
Ethical approval was obtained from Osun State Health Research Ethical Committee  (OSHREC/PRS/five hundred sixty-nineTthree hundred twelve/ on the twenty-second of May twenty twenty-three.
Malaria test positivity was determined by rapid diagnostic test (RDT)  and microscopy.
In addition, haemoglobin levels were measured using Haemocue® Hb two hundred one.
Caregivers were interviewed  on malaria management practices using tools adapted from Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey.
Results A total of four hundred children aged two–eighteen months were assessed in this study, which was conducted  in July twenty twenty-three.

Conclusion Malaria infection and anaemia were found to be higher in older children.
Household wealth and child’s  age were significantly associated with malaria infection.
These findings would inform the positioning of PMC interven tion touch-points to reduce malaria burden in young children.
It is the primary cause of morbidity  and mortality for this age group, with over ninety-five thousand deaths  from malaria annually [two].
In addition, there are ongoing efforts to pro vide evidence for the implementation of perennial malaria  chemoprevention (PMC) [five].
The children at high-risk of malaria infection can be  given antimalarial medicines at predefined intervals to  prevent transmission.
The strategy recommends using expanded  programme on immunization (EPI) as the platform for  delivering PMC.
To support decision-making at the  country level, PMC recommendation must be accompa nied by available research evidence.
The WHO encourages acquisition of evidence in the local context, before  national malaria programmes’ adoption, adaptation and  scale-up [six].
Women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years)  were interviewed and their children aged two–eighteen months  recruited for biomarker testing.

Four hundred (four hundred) children  were randomly selected across eighty clusters/communities (five (five) from each cluster/community) in eight LGAs.
T he data collectors mobilized the eligible children from  selected households, to a designated centre within  the community.
At this centre, a team of laboratory  scientists collected blood samples from the children.
One child was randomly selected  per household.
The five (five) children sampled from each  cluster/community were tested for malaria and anaemia.
Study population(s) questionnaire T hree questionnaires were utilized based on the study  objectives.
These include name, sex, age, residency  status, and line number.
The respondent to this questionnaire  was usually the head of the household.
In addition, the household  questionnaire collected information on ownership  and use of bed nets.
All women aged fifteen–forty-nine years  identified in the household were interviewed.
Child questionnaire captured basic information  about every child selected for the study.
Information  such as age, sex, history of fever, malaria, hospital  admission due to malaria amongst others were  captured.
A pre-and post-test was conducted to  analyse the training impact.

Data collection The data collection was conducted July twenty twenty-three.
In addition, sociodemographic and clinical information were  captured for all children that were randomly selected.
This included their age, sex, height, weight, temperature,  haemoglobin concentration, positive or negative malaria  test results by RDT.
Blood samples were collected from all  eligible children whose caregivers gave written informed  consent.
Histidine-Rich  Protein two (HRPtwo) RDT was conducted according to  manufacturer’s manual and blood spotted on the filter  paper according to the SOP.
The filter papers were air  dried and stored individually in plastic sleeves with seal locks with desiccant sachets.
These blood spot samples  are currently stored at room temperature away from  extreme light and heat for future parasite genotyping  assays (NGS).
Haemoglobin concentration assessed with  concentration  lesser than seven.
Zero g/dl and those with malaria infection  were referred to the nearest health facility for treatment  [nine].
Thin films of duplicate blood slides for microscopy  were fixed and the films stained with three percent Giemsa for one h.
Data management and statistical analysis T he household wealth tertile was computed using the  principal components analysis (PCA) technique.
Then, the factor loadings and z-scores were calculated.
For each  household, the indicator values were multiplied by the  loadings and summed to produce the household’s wealth  index value.
The standardized z-score was used to classify  the overall scores to wealth tertile (poor, medium, rich).
Data was collected and entered into Microsoft Excel and  exported to Stata Version sixteen (StataCorp; College Station,  TX, USA) for further analysis.
Counts, percentage and descriptive statistics were used for univariate estimates.
The prevalence of malaria parasites was expressed in  percentage.
For bivariate analysis, Chi-square test was  used.
The variable(s) statistically significant at p  lesser than zero.
Five were included in the multivariable logistic regression.
A multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to  examine the factors associated with malaria infection  among children aged two–eighteen months.
Laboratory analysis Malaria microscopy slides were stained in the field and  later read in the NIMR laboratory.
The microscopy results  such as detection, species, stage, gametocyte detection,  asexual parasite count, gametocyte count were included.
During data analysis, the children household data were  linked by the unique identifier to the samples collected  for malariometric assessment.
The slides were examined  at a magnification of a one thousand X binocular light microscope  and the parasites counted [ten].
Slides were considered negative if no parasite was detected  after reading two hundred high-powered fields.
The presence  of gametocytes was also recorded.
Thin blood smears  were reviewed for non P. falciparum infections.
Two  microscopists read all slides independently, and parasite  densities were calculated by averaging the two counts.
Definition of anaemia Haemoglobin levels were calculated to determine the  anaemia status.
A Hb reading of Hb  lesser than seven.

Zero percent) among children thirteen–eighteen months.

It was however higher than the result obtained for Osun  state in the twenty twenty-one NMIS [fourteen].
Though malaria prevalence  dropped from forty-two percent in twenty ten to twenty-one.
There was a shift of  medical resources from malaria control to emergency COVID-nineteen response during the pandemic.
This caused  disruptions, reductions, and delays in malaria prevention  and control interventions.
By implication, malaria prevention and control  interventions must be sustained to prevent resurgence.

Identifying  associated factors, such as socioeconomic status,  environmental conditions, and healthcare access, can  inform targeted strategies.
Studies should explore spatial–temporal patterns of  malaria prevalence to identify hotspots and guide  targeted interventions.
Evaluating community-based interventions and integrating malaria  control with other child health programs is essential for  sustainable progress.
This study was household-based and gives a broad  overview of the malariometric situation across selected  LGAs in Osun State.
The randomly selection of clusters  or communities, households and children, gives a  balance to the endogenous and exogenous factors.
A key limitation is  that cross-sectional study cannot be used to established  causality.
The prevalence of malaria and anaemia among children  aged seven–eighteen months were higher compared to younger  children in their first six months of life.
Malaria was also associated with child’s age and household wealth tertile.
These findings would inform the positioning of PMC  intervention touch points to reduce malaria burden in  young children.

This study assessed malaria  prevention knowledge and its utilisation among pregnant  women in Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria.
Results showed good knowledge but low utilisation of preventive measures  among pregnant women.
Factors such as education and occupation were linked to better understanding, while religion  had no significant impact.
Trimester and gravidity also influenced knowledge levels.
Investigating health  interventions and community engagement could improve  malaria prevention efforts.
[thirty-two] As such, this study results may  not be applicable to broader populations in respect to context specific situations.

INTRODUCTION  Malaria remains one of the most crucial life-threat ening parasitic diseases in tropical and subtropical regions [one].
It is caused by Plasmodium parasites,  which are primarily transmitted through the bites  of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes [two].
In twenty twenty-two, Nigeria reported an estimated sixty-eight million  malaria cases and one hundred ninety-four thousand malaria-related deaths  [three].
Plasmodium falciparum has developed mecha nisms such as antigenic switching to evade im mune responses, resulting in significant gene di versity.
This genetic diversity often complicates the  development of effective vaccines and control  strategies [six].
Common genetic markers in P. Faciparum.
Eight Olorunfemi et al.
MWJ twenty twenty-five, sixteen:eight https://doi.
Termining malaria transmission in a community [eight].
Their genetic diversity also contributes to P.Faciparum.
Falci parum's ability to evade the host's immune system  and develop resistance to antimalarial drugs.
This protein, comprising seventeen twenty amino  acids, is organised into seventeen blocks with varying lev els of conservation [ten].
Block two of msp-one is highly  variable, comprising three allelic families: Kone,  MADtwenty, and ROthirty-three.
The msp-two alleles are classified into  two dimorphic families, FCtwenty-seven and threeDseven [eleven].
HIV-induced  immunosuppression increases susceptibility to op portunistic infections, including malaria [fourteen].
This, in turn,  could elevate the risk of severe complications such  as cerebral malaria and severe anaemia.
Further more, parasite genetic diversity might indicate less  pressure for drug resistance mutations.
The co-in fection of malaria and HIV poses a significant pub lic health challenge, especially in regions where  malaria is endemic [fifteen].
PLWH have a higher risk  of contracting malaria and are more likely to expe rience severe disease manifestations and complica tions.
Conversely, malaria has been shown to accel erate HIV progression by increasing viral replica tion rates [sixteen].
However, despite high malaria and HIV preva lence, limited research exists on malaria genetic diversity in PLWH in Nigeria.

Study design and population This was a cross-sectional, health facility-based  study investigating the genetic diversity of P.Faciparum
Falciparum among HIV patients attending the HIV care  center at the study site.
Samples were collected be tween December twenty twenty-one and January twenty twenty-three.
The study employed a convenience sampling method for  sample collection.
Patients above eighteen years old and who consented to the survey were included in  the study.
Patients below eighteen years, those who had  recently used antimalarial drugs within two weeks  two April twenty twenty-five,  Vol.

Of sample collection, and those who did not con sent were excluded from the study.
The research was carried out  following the Code of Ethics of the World Medical  Association (Helsinki Declaration) [nineteen].
Informed  written or verbal (from uneducated) consent was  obtained from all participants.
Sample collection and malaria diagnosis Participants were tested for malaria using the  Rapid Diagnostic Test Kit (SD BIOLINE Malaria).
F/Pan) during the interview.
The test was per formed in the field and interpreted within twenty min utes, following the manufacturer's instructions.
Dried blood spots (DBS) were collected by finger  prick and spotted directly onto labeled threeMM  Whatman filter paper.
Simultaneously, thick blood  smears were prepared for each participant.
These  smears were examined microscopically to assess  malaria parasite density using Giemsa staining.
Parasite density was quantified in parasites/µL,  based on an assumed average of eight thousand leukocytes  per microlitre of blood [twenty].
One–one parasite/µL),  discordant cases were classified based on PCR con f irmation.
A second expert microscopist re-exam ined a subset of slides to ensure accuracy.
DNA was extracted from DBS on filter pa per using the QIAamp Mini DNA extraction kit  (QIAGEN, USA), following the manufacturer's in structions.
Sixty microliters of DNA were eluted  and stored at -twenty °C until further analysis.
PCR was conducted on all samples, regard less of microscopy results.
Two sets of genus- and  species-specific primers (P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. knowlesi
(P.ovale, and P. vivax) were used as described previ ously [twenty-one].
DNA was amplified using nested PCR  to enable specific species identification across po tential sequence variations.
A final extension was performed at seventy-two °C for five minutes.
The PCR products were analysed using  gel electrophoresis on a one.
Two percent agarose gel and visu alised under a UV transilluminator.
Fragment sizes  were compared against a one hundred base pair Solis Bio dyne DNA ladder.
Amplification of block two of msp-one, block three  of msp-two, and glurp genes was performed using two  rounds of nested PCR as previously described [twenty-two].
The outer regions of the two genes were initially  amplified, followed by a nested PCR with allelic  family-specific primer pairs.
A final extension was performed at seventy-two °C  for five minutes.
A final extension step was  performed at seventy-two °C for three minutes.
For the glurp  gene, a semi-nested PCR reaction targeting the  polymorphic Rtwo region was performed in a final  volume of twenty-five µL using specific primers.
The cycling  conditions for both reactions were the same, except  the annealing temperature for the second reaction  was set to fifty-nine °C.
PCR products were analysed via gel elec trophoresis on a one.
Two percent agarose gel and visualised  under a UV transilluminator.
Fragment sizes were  determined relative to a one hundred bp DNA ladder using  the Azure bioimaging system.

DISCUSSION Co-infection of HIV with malaria poses a substan tial global health challenge, especially in malaria endemic regions.
Understanding the genetic struc ture of the malaria parasite population can com plement malaria control interventions.
This study  six April twenty twenty-five,  Vol.

Provides information on the genetic diversity of P.ovale
Falciparum among PLWH in Ogbomoso, Nigeria.
The high prevalence of malaria observed in this study underscores the complexity of malaria  epidemiology in the study region.
The presence of P. falciparum or P. malariae in the population is  noteworthy.

This strategy has demonstrated protective benefits  against malaria regardless of CDfour count or clinical  stage [twenty-five].
However, prolonged exposure of Plas modium species to CTX could reduce its effective ness, contributing to persistent infections among  PLWH.

The PCR results demonstrate the value of molecular tech niques in accurately identifying infections that may  be missed by microscopy or RDT.
The analysis re vealed no significant differences in malaria preva lence across demographic characteristics when us ing RDT.
However, significant differences were ob served with microscopy, particularly in infections  caused by P. falciparum.
Additionally, the  significant differences observed with microscopy in  infections caused by both P. falciparum and P.

The study showed substantial genetic diversity.
The distribution of allelic families (Kone, MADtwenty, and  ROthirty-three) in msp-one indicates a balanced representation  of these families in the population.
This is contrary  to most studies reporting a high prevalence of Kone  allelic family [thirty-one-thirty-two].
The majority of alleles identi f ied for msp-two belong to the FCtwenty-seven family.
This is  similar to the study conducted in Grande Comore  Island [thirty-three], where most of the isolates belong to the  FCtwenty-seven family.
This dominance suggests spatial dy namics in the genetic profile of P. falciparum popula tions among the study population.
The MOI for msp-one (two.
Two) suggests a rela tively high level of genetic diversity in the parasite  population.
The genetic diversity observed aligns  with high malaria transmission rates in Nigeria and  most sub-Saharan African countries [thirty-five].
A high  MOI of P. falciparum has been suggested to increase  the risk of clinical outcomes of malaria parasite in fections.
In contrast, the MOI for msp-two (one.
Thirteen) and  glurp gene (one.
Zero) indicates a more stable population  with fewer distinct alleles per infection.
The overall  MOI of one.
Thirty-eight reflects a mixed infection scenario that  may influence disease severity and treatment out comes.

Eighty-six), suggesting significant genetic diversity, which may  impact the immune response of individuals.

CONCLUSIONS This study demonstrates a low prevalence of Plas modium falciparum and its genetic diversity among  PLWH in Ogbomoso, Nigeria.
Despite the high  malaria transmission intensity in this region, the  overall genetic diversity of P. falciparum was low.
At  the msp-two loci, most infections are monoclonal, lim iting antigenic markers' effectiveness as genotyping  tools for tracking drug efficacy.

Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs)  The NxTek Ultra-sensitive Malaria Ag P. falciparum RDT and the SD Bioline™ Malaria Ag P.
Falciparum RDT were employed to detect malaria HRPtwo Pf in patient blood samples following the  manufacturer's instructions.
Results were read after twenty  minutes for NxTek and fifteen minutes for SD Bioline™.
A line in the ‘C’ window indicated a valid test,  with a positive result if a line appeared in the P. falciparum-line (Pf-line) window.
An adjacent line to  “C” indicated a negative result.
If no line appeared adjacent to “C”, the test was considered invalid and  repeated using a new cassette.
The presence of a Pf-line was confirmed by two independent assistants,  with a third person consulted in case of uncertainty.
The person conducting the RDTs was blinded to the  reference test results.
RDT kits were stored at the recommended temperature ( lesser thanforty°C), and the validity of  each kit was certified by laboratory scientists before use.
Data analysis  The data collected was entered into Statistical Product and Service Solutions (SPSS) version twenty-five.

Privacy was ensured  for the study population, and all information supplied was handled confidentially.

Methods An open-label, randomised controlled clinical trial was conducted.
The participants were randomised into  two treatment groups using simple randomisation by computer-generated random numbers.
They had either artemether lumefantrine (AL) or dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine phosphate (DHAPQ) for three days.
The participants were  monitored for forty-two days by examining blood films for malaria parasite density on days one, two, three, seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, thirty-five, and forty-two.
Malaria parasite genotyping by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was done to differentiate between reinfection and  recrudescence.

Thin and thick films for malaria parasites were pre pared, fixed and stained by the two study microscopists  [twenty-five].
The microscopists examined each slide indepen dently using a light microscope at a magnification of  ×one thousand.
The parasite density was obtained by finding the  average of the two counts.
In case of discordance of  greater than twenty-five percent  in the parasite density, the slide was re-examined by a  malaria parasitologist.
The parasite density was deter mined as the average of the two most consistent counts.
A slide was deemed to be parasite-negative after two hundred  microscope fields were examined, and no parasite was  detected [twenty-five].
After allocating the participants into treat ment categories, the microscopists were blinded to treat ment allocation.

Discussion This study found that AL and DHAPQ were efficacious  in the treatment of malaria in children with an ACPR  cure rate that exceeds ninety percent.
Reinfection, not recrudes cence, was the cause of the seven treatment failures that  the participants had.

This is in the spirit  of using every consultation as an opportunity for health  promotion and disease prevention.
This will  significantly lessen the burden of malaria when used with  improved diagnosis and effective vector control.
In this study, the Day-three parasite positivity was five percent (ninety-five percent  CI of one.
Nine) in the AL group and three.
Seven) in the DHAPQ treatment group.
This high Day-three  parasite positivity may be due to the higher baseline par asite density observed among the participants.
Parasite  clearance is relatively slower in the face of a high parasite  load [forty-one].
Four percent of participants in the AL and DHAPQ, respectively,  ruled out the possibility of artemisinin resistance in the  study area.
T he high mean parasite clearance time of sixty-one.
Forty-two h among the participants in the AL and  DHAPQ groups, respectively, may invariably be due to  the higher initial parasite load.
Similarly high mean par asite clearance times have been reported by other stud ies [twenty-six, forty-three, forty-four].
These studies were conducted during the  rainy season when malaria transmission is higher.
The  mean fever clearance time was significantly lower in the  AL group compared to the DHAPQ group (forty-six.
This was similar to what was  obtained in a survey done in Senegal [forty-five].
This value was,  however, higher than those observed in other studies  where antipyretics were used in the management of fever  [forty-three, forty-six].
The use of antipyretics can mask fever and give a  lower fever clearance time.
These  findings are in tandem with those reported from other  trials [twenty-six, forty-five, forty-seven, forty-eight].
Artemisinin resistance mani fests clinically as ETF, while partner drug resistance man ifests as LCF or LPF [fifty].
T he findings from the comparative tolerability of AL  and DHAPQ were not surprising.
DHAPQ was less well tolerated than  AL, with five participants having mild adverse events in  the form of vomiting, body itching, and abdominal pain.
Limitations A major limitation of this study is that the patients were  not admitted, and the evening doses of AL were not  directly observed.
This may have led to missed unre ported doses and an underestimation of the efficacy  of AL.
To mitigate against this risk, the caregivers were  reminded daily to take their medications throughout the  study duration.
Admitting the study participants would  also reduce the risk of reinfection.
Reinfection and recrudescence rates could  vary in a larger and more diverse population sample.
Nevertheless, caution is warranted in  Ahmed et al.
Similarly, DHAPQ was also found  to have good parasite clearance.
However, no significant  statistical difference was observed between their efficacy.
It recommended health education of caregivers of under f ive children on malaria prevention and continuous effi cacy monitoring of the drugs.

Gm Abstract Nigeria continues to face a serious public health problem due to malaria, which contrib utes around twenty-sevenpercent of all cases worldwide.
Although insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) are essential interventions for preventing malaria, their use in Nigeria is still sub-optimal.
Understanding the factors influencing ITN use is essential to improve malaria control strat egies.
This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of and factors associated with ITN use among women of reproductive age in Nigeria.
We conducted a secondary data anal ysis of the twenty twenty-one Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS).
The sample included fourteen thousand, four hundred seventy-six women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years) from five hundred sixty-seven clusters across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones.
Multilevel logistic regression was used to examine the contextual factors associated with ITN use, accounting for both fixed and random effects.
Statistical significance was set at plesser thanzero.
Five, with ninety-fivepercent confidence intervals reported for all estimates.
The weighted prevalence of ITN use was forty-one.
The results showed Muslim women had twenty-onepercent (a OR equal to zero).
Ninety-four) lower odds of ITN use, when compared with the Chris tian women.
Those who had living children were more likely to report ITN use, when com pared with women with no child.
The non-poor women had higher odds of ITN use, when compared with the poor women (aORequal to one.
In addition, women from multi-ethnic had twenty-sixpercent lower odds of ITN use, when compared with those from mono-ethnic community (aORequal to zero.
The geographical region was significantly associated with ITN use among Nigerian women.
Low-level community poverty (aORequal to zero.
ITN use among women of reproductive age in Nigeria remained below the national target.
Interventions to increase ITN use should consider the complex interplay of individual and community-level factors.
Introduction Malaria remains a critical global health challenge, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing a dis proportionate burden globally.
In twenty twenty-one, the region accounted for approximately ninety-fivepercent of two hundred forty-seven million global malaria cases and ninety-sixpercent of six hundred nineteen thousand malaria-related deaths [one].
Nigeria, in particular, has the highest malaria burden, representing approximately twenty-sevenpercent of global cases and thirty-twopercent of deaths [two].
This impact extends beyond health, imposing a significant economic burden on Nigeria, estimated at approximately one.
Onepercent of the country’s GDP [three].
Women of reproductive age are especially vulnerable and face increased risks of severe anemia, mater nal mortality, and adverse birth outcomes [forty-five].
In malaria-endemic areas, this demographic group experiences a higher infection prevalence compared to non-pregnant women and adult men [sixty-seven].
Recognizing the effectiveness of ITNs, global and regional policy frameworks have empha sized increasing ITN coverage and use.
The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG three.
Three, call for ending the malaria epidemic by twenty thirty [eleven].
Despite these commitments and substantial investments in ITN distribution, utilization rates remain suboptimal.
A multi-country analysis of twenty-nine sub-Saharan African countries found two / fourteen PLOS Global Public Health https://doi.who.malaria.org
Women of reproductive age play a pivotal role in household decision-making regarding health practices, including ITN use [twenty-four].
Methods Data source We used individual woman questionnaire data from the twenty twenty-one Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS).
In total, fourteen thousand, four hundred seventy-six women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years) made up the study’s sample that was analyzed.
The data collection took place from twelve October to four December twenty twenty-one.
Nigeria is separated into states administra tively.
Local government areas (LGAs) are the lowest level of governance in each state.
Within LGAs are wards, and within wards are localities.
Census enumeration areas (EAs), which are handy areas, are further subdivided into localities.
Based on the EAs for the projected twenty twenty-three PHC, the primary sampling unit (PSU), also known as a cluster unit for the twenty twenty-one NMIS, was defined.
For the NMIS of twenty twenty-one, a two-phase sampling approach was chosen.
A probability proportional to the EA size was used to choose five hundred sixty-eight EAs in the first stage.
The number of households inside an EA determines its size.
The sample was chosen in a way that made it representative of every state.
As a consequence, there were five hundred sixty-eight clusters nationwide - one hundred ninety-five of which were in urban areas and three hundred seventy-three of which were in rural areas.
Between August twenty-six, twenty twenty-one, and September eighteen, twenty twenty-one, all of the households in these clusters were listed in full.
The lists of homes that were produced were used as the sample frame to choose the households for the second stage.
In the twenty twenty-one NMIS sample, GPS dongles were utilised to record coordinates during the households listing process [twenty-seven].
By using equal probability systematic sampling, twenty-five households from each cluster were chosen for the second step of the selection procedure.
The datasets are available in the public domain via https://dhsprogram.org
Com/data/dataset/Nigeria_MIS_twenty twenty-one.
Selection and measurements of variables Outcome variable.
The outcome variable in the study was ITN use.
It was derived from the question variable “Vfour hundred sixty-one - Respondent slept under mosquito bed net”.
This yielded three/fourteen PLOS Global Public Health https://doi.who.malaria.org
This follows the operational definition of ITN use as used by NMIS [twenty-seven].
The MIS twenty twenty-one provides current and comprehensive data on malaria-related indicators, including ITN use.
Explanatory variables.
Previous studies provided the basis for the factors this study examined [twenty-eight–thirty].
Analytical approach.
Stata software version seventeen.
Zero (Stata Corporation, College Station, Texas, USA) was used for data analysis.
Percentage was employed in the univariable analysis.
The fixed and random effects of ITN use were investigated using the multilevel multivariable binary logistic regression.
In order to assess multicollinearity, which is known to raise serious issues with the logit model, the variance inflation factor was employed [thirty-one].
We built four models.
First, the community-level variance was computed in the empty or unconditional model with no explanatory factors.
We used the results to justify the multilevel statistical model.
Since the variance was statistically significant, the use of multilevel regression was established.
The second model included the individual-level factors, the third model included the community-level factors.
Finally, the fourth model (full model) adjusted for the individual and community-level factors.
The level of significance was determined at p lesser than zero.
To choose the best model from the four models, the Bayesian and Akaike Informa tion Criteria were used.
A lower Akaike or Bayesian Information Criterion value denotes a better model fit [thirty-two].
Fixed and random effects.
The Intra-class Correlation (ICC) and Median Odds Ratio (MOR) were used to quantify the likely contextual effects [thirty-three].
With the use of ICC, we assessed the similarity between respondents living in the same community.
The MOR estimated the median increase in odds of ITN use if a woman moved to a community with higher ITN use probability.
This approach allowed us to distinguish between individual-level variation and community-level influence on ITN use patterns.

Tthree PLOS GLObaL PubLic HeaLtH ITN use among women in Nigeria twenty twenty-five [ten].
The prevalence we observed is consistent with other studies in similar settings, such as the forty-three.
Twopercent ITN use reported among adults in northern Ethiopia [thirty-five].
This difference could be attributed to targeted interventions focusing on maternal health and increased risk perception in this population [thirty-six].
Socioeconomic and demographic factors emerged as significant predictors of ITN use in our study [thirty-seven].
Wealth status played a crucial role, with non-poor women having thirty-fivepercent higher odds of using ITNs compared to their poor counterparts.
Interestingly, our study found that women with children were more likely to use ITNs, with odds increasing with the number of living children.
Religious affiliation and ethnic diversity have emerged as significant belief and cultural factors influencing ITN use.
Muslim women had twenty-onepercent lower odds of ITN use compared to Christian women, a finding that echoes recent research in Nigeria [forty-five].
This disparity might be rooted in differing health beliefs, social norms, or access to health information across religious groups [forty-six].
The lower likelihood of ITN use in multi-ethnic communities compared to mono-ethnic ones (OR equal to zero.
Ninety-four]) is a novel finding that warrants further investigation.
Community-level factors played a substantial role in determining ITN use, accounting for twenty-fourpercent of the total variance in the model.
This finding aligns with recent multi-country analyses that have highlighted the importance of community context in health behaviors [twenty-three].
Interestingly, community education level did not show a significant association with ITN use, in con trast to some recent studies [thirty-nine].
The substantial community- level variation observed in our study (ICC equal to zero.
Sixty-four) emphasizes the need for community-focused interventions to complement individual-targeted strategies to promote ITN use [fifty-one].
Nine/fourteen PLOS Global Public Health https://doi.getmalaria.info.com
However, this study had some limitations.
The cross-sectional nature of NMIS data precludes the establishment of causal relationships between the identified factors and ITN use.
There may be recall bias in self-reported ITN use, potentially leading to over- or underestimation of actual usage.
Conclusion The findings revealed that despite progress, ITN utilization remains suboptimal, with less than half of the target population using ITNs.

According to the World Malaria Report, there were two hundred forty-nine million cases globally in eighty-five malaria endemic coun tries in twenty twenty-three.
Nigeria was first among the twenty-nine countries accounting for ninety-fivepercent of the global cases, and first (at thirty-one.
Onepercent) among the four countries accounting for nearly half of all malaria deaths worldwide in twenty twenty-two [two].
Between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-two, there was an increase of about five.
Three million estimated cases in the country [two].
Out of thirty-six states and the Federal Capital Territory, Kebbi State contributed an estimated three.
Onepercent of the sixty-eight million malaria cases in twenty twenty-one, and children under five years accounted for forty-ninepercent of the cases.
This makes Kebbi the state with the highest malaria burden in Nigeria [three, four].
Malaria burden is driven by multiple factors rang ing from socioeconomic to ecological.
Leading rice producing areas in Nigeria are Kebbi (the major producer in northern Nigeria), Borno, Kano, and Kaduna [eight, nine] states.
Traditional rain-fed rice farming in Kebbi has been driven by rainfall and suitable ‘tableland’ topography, which encourages water retention.
By providing suitable and produc tive larval habitats [fourteen], rice farming has been linked to increased malaria prevalence.
In Nigeria, insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) are the major vector control strategy.
Kebbi State conducted mass ITN distribution campaigns in twenty fourteen and twenty eighteen, and most recently twenty twenty-two, with between three and three.
Five million ITNs distributed in each campaign.
Despite data from the Nigeria Malaria Indicator Sur vey in twenty twenty-one indicating that seventy-threepercent of households in Kebbi owned an ITN, only thirty-eight.
Twopercent slept under an ITN the night before the survey [fifteen].
Methods Study area Kebbi State is in the northwestern part of Nigeria (twelve).
With a total landmass of about thirty-seven thousand, six hundred ninety-nine kmtwo, over a third of which is farmland, and with an estimated population of four.
Four million as of twenty sixteen (National Population Commission of Nigeria, twenty sixteen).
The land scape is dominated by extensive flood plains (fadama) of the inland river valley systems.
Both rivers have broad flood plains.
The f low of the Rima River is, however, constant and reaches its peak during the short rainy season between June and September.
T he LSM habitat survey was carried out in Argungu, Bunza and Kalgo LGAs in Kebbi State between July and August twenty twenty-two (Fig.
One, which cover a land mass of about ten forty-two kmtwo, ten thirty-four kmtwo, and five hundred ninety-nine kmtwo, respectively.
The LGAs were selected due to high malaria incidence rates, availability of larval habitats, community acceptance and stable security.
Mean annual rainfall varies significantly from the northern part of the state (seven hundred thirty-three mm) to the southern part (ten forty-five mm).
The average number of rainy days also var ies, from fifty days in the north to eighty days in the south.
Monthly average rainfall ranges from one.
Thirty-four mm across the three LGAs, while monthly average tempera tures range from twenty-four.

Global Positioning System coordinates of sampled sites were recorded using the mobile device.
Locations where only one or two out of the ten dips taken contained Anopheles sp.
Larvae were regarded as having low density.
Locations where no Anopheles sp.
Larvae could be found in ten dips were regarded as negative or empty [twenty-three].
Mean larval density for each location was calculated by dividing the total number of larvae by ten dips.
All Anopheles mos quito larvae collected in the field were sorted to remove the predators.
The immature larvae were reared in larval bowls covered with nets.
These were categorized into two: the proportion within a distance greater than one hundred m and lesser than one hundred m.
This was calculated to establish the proximity of the breeding site to human dwellings.
Productivity of larval habitats in Argungu, Bunza and Kalgo LGAs were determined using the breeding index calculations.
Abundance of each larval habitat identified in the three LGAs was compared using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).
Chi-square tests were applied to compare the significance of the proportion of larval habi tat within one hundred m and greater than or equal to one hundred m from human habitations.

This study examined the prevalence and determinants of insecticide-treated net (ITN) ownership among women of reproductive age in Nigeria.
Methods The individual woman questionnaire data from the twenty twenty-one Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS) was used.
In total, fourteen thousand, four hundred seventy-six women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years) made up the study’s sample that was analysed.
The outcome variable in the study was ITN ownership.
Percentage and multivariable multilevel binary logistic regression model were estimated at p lesser than zero.
Results The weighted prevalence of ITN ownership was sixty-two.
Women aged twenty-five–thirty-four and thirty-five–forty-nine had twelvepercent (aOR equal to zero.
Ninety-eight) and sixteenpercent (aOR equal to zero.
Ninety-seven) reduction in ITN ownership, when compared with women aged fifteen–twenty-four years.
Women who had one–two (aOR equal to one.
Forty-six) and five and above living children (aOR equal to one.
Fifty-eight), had higher odds of ITN ownership when compared with those with no living child respectively.
Women from non-poor households had higher odds of ITN ownership, when compared with their poor counterparts (aOR equal to one.
Women from North East (aOR equal to four.
Sixty-three) and North West (aOR equal to four.
One) had higher odds of ITN ownership, while those from South East (aOR equal to zero.
Sixty-two) and South South (aOR equal to zero.
Eighty-five) had reductions in the odds of ITN ownership, when compared with women from North Central respectively.
Conclusion Approximately two-third of Nigerian women reported ITN ownership.
This underscore the need for targeted interventions to address barriers and improve ITN access.
While free ITN distribution programmes have been effective, socioeconomic and demographic factors have remained contributory to ITN access.

In response to this public health issue, the use of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) has been identified as a critical preventive measure.
Over the last decade, the Nigerian government and its partners have undertaken several malaria preventive programmes.
ITN provide a physical barrier against mosquitoes, reducing human-vector contact, and are treated with insecticides that kill or repel mosquitoes.
The use of ITNs has been shown to significantly reduce malaria incidence, morbidity, and mortality [five].
Regardless of insecticide treatment, bed nets create a physical barrier that reduces mosquito-human interaction and successful blood feeding.
This can provide communal protection in addition to personal effects.
High insecticide-treated bed nets can also reduce adult mosquito density and alter the mosquito population’s age distribution.
Lately, however, the decrease in malaria morbidity and mortality has stalled [seven, eight].
Some suggest that this inertia is due to increasing resistance in malaria vectors to the pyrethroid insecticides used for treating ITNs.
Understanding the prevalence and determinants of ITN ownership is crucial for the effective implementation of malaria control programmes.
Women are particularly vulnerable to malaria.
ITN ownership among women is critical for reducing malaria transmission, especially in regions with high malaria prevalence.
ITNs are one of the most effective tools for preventing malaria by protecting individuals from mosquito bites.
Rural women, those with lower education, and poorer households are less likely to own ITNs [nine].
This study explores the prevalence and factors associated with ITN ownership among women in Nigeria.
Methods Data source T he individual woman questionnaire data from the twenty twenty-one Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS) was used.
In total, fourteen thousand, four hundred seventy-six women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years) made up the study’s sample that was analysed.
The data collection took place from twelve October to four December twenty twenty-one.
Nigeria’s geopolitical zones where the data was collected are as follows: North Central: Benue, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Niger, Plateau, and FCT.
North East: Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba, and Yobe.
North West: Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto, and Zamfara.
South East: Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, and Imo.
South South: Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Edo, and Rivers.
South West: Ekiti, Lagos, Ogun, Osun, Ondo, and Oyo.
Nigeria is separated into states administratively.
Local government areas (LGAs) are the lowest level of governance in each state.
Within LGAs are wards, and within wards are localities.
Census enumeration areas (EAs), which are handy areas, are further subdivided into localities.
Based on the EAs for the projected twenty twenty-three PHC, the primary sampling unit (PSU), also known as a cluster unit for the twenty twenty-one NMIS, was defined.
For the NMIS of twenty twenty-one, a two-phase sampling approach was chosen.
A probability proportional to the EA size was used to choose five hundred sixty-eight EAs in the first stage.
Malaria Journal Page three of nine The number of households inside an EA determines its size.
The sample was chosen in a way that made it representative of every state.
As a consequence, there were five hundred sixty-eight clusters nationwide—one hundred ninety-five of which were in urban areas and three hundred seventy-three of which were in rural areas.
Between August twenty-six, twenty twenty-one, and September eighteen, twenty twenty-one, all of the households in these clusters were listed in full.
The lists of homes that were produced were used as the sample frame to choose the households for the second stage.
In the twenty twenty-one NMIS sample, GPS dongles were utilized to record coordinates during the households listing process [ten].
By using equal probability systematic sampling, twenty-five households from each cluster were chosen for the second step of the selection procedure.
The datasets are available in the public domain via https://dhsprogram.org
Com/data/dataset/Nigeria_ MIS_twenty twenty-one.
Selection and measurements of variables Outcome variables The outcome variable in the study was ITN ownership.
It was derived from the question variable “Vfour hundred fifty-nine—Have mosquito bed net for sleeping”.
This yielded a binary response, with ‘yes’ coded as “one” indicating that the respondent had ITN, and ‘no’ coded as “zero” indicating otherwise.
This follows the operational definition of ITN ownership as used by NMIS [ten].
The MIS twenty twenty-one provides current and comprehensive data on malaria related indicators, including ITN ownership.
Analytical approach Stata software version seventeen.
Zero (Stata Corporation, College Station, Texas, USA) was used for data analysis.
Percentage was employed in the univariable analysis.
The fixed and random effects of ITN ownership were investigated using the multilevel multivariable binary logistic regression.
In order to assess multicollinearity, which is known to raise serious issues with the logit model, the variance inflation factor was employed [fifteen].
Four models were built.
First, the community-level variance was computed in the empty or unconditional model, which included no explanatory factors.
The null model served as a benchmark to assess the extent to which community characteristics accounted for the observed changes.
The results justified the use of a multilevel statistical model.
Since the variance was statistically significant, the use of multilevel regression was established.
The second model included individual-level factors, and the third model included community-level factors.
Finally, the fourth model (full model) adjusted for the individual and community-level factors.
The level of significance was determined at p lesser than zero.
To choose the best model from the four models, the Bayesian and Akaike Information Criteria were used.
A lower Akaike or Bayesian Information Criterion value denotes a better model fit [sixteen].
The Intra class Correlation (ICC) and Median Odds Ratio (MOR) were used to quantify the likely contextual effects [seventeen].
The ICC was used to assess the similarity between respondents living in the same community.
The ICC is a measure of the clustering of odds of ITN ownership in the same community.
It shows the percentage of the total variance in the likelihood of ITN ownership that is connected to the community-level factors.
Furthermore, when the MOR is one, there is no variance in communities.
Ethical consideration T he de-identified public secondary dataset was used for this study.
The respondents’ informed consent was collected by NMIS in accordance with standard ethical protocol.
The authors were granted permission to use the data, therefore no further participants’ agreement or consent was required.
The details of DHS ethical guidelines can be found here: http:// goo.com
Results T he weighted prevalence of ITN ownership was sixty-two.
Figure one showed that two-third of Nigerian women reported ITN ownership.
Significant differences in ITN ownership prevalence were observed for several variables, as indicated by their p-values.
Young women aged fifteen–twenty-four years had the highest prevalence of ITN ownership (sixty-four.
One) compared to those aged twenty-five–thirty-four (sixty-two.
Five) and thirty-five–forty-nine years (sixty.
Zero), with a significant p-value of zero.
Women with no formal education or only primary education had significantly higher ITN ownership (sixty-eight.
One) compared to those with secondary or higher education (fifty-six.
Religion was also significantly associated with ITN ownership (p lesser than zero.
Muslim women reported the highest ITN ownership (seventy.
One), compared to Christian women (fifty-one.
Additionally, households headed by males had a significantly higher prevalence of ITN ownership (sixty-four.

Discussion The study examined the prevalence and factors associated with ITN ownership among women of reproductive age in Nigeria.
The study found that sixty-two.
Sixpercent of Nigerian women of reproductive age own an ITN, with a ninety-fivepercent Confidence Interval (CI) of sixty.
Our study’s prevalence of ownership is similar to a community study in the south-western part of Nigeria [twenty].
Sixpercent ownership of an ITN among women of reproductive age could be attributed to free distribution of ITNs, as most ITNs are obtained for free.
However, there is need to improve malaria prevention coverage especially in areas with lower ITN coverage and addressing barriers to access ITN.
This highlights potential gaps in malaria prevention efforts and health equity.
Addressing these factors through targeted and context-specific interventions could help bridge the gap in ITN ownership across different age groups.
Ensuring that all age groups have equitable access to ITNs is crucial for effective malaria control and improving overall public health outcomes.
Number of living children for Women (women who had children had higher odds of insecticide treated net ownership.
Similar findings were documented in an analysis of the twenty eighteen Demographic and Health Survey of Guinea [twenty-two].
Public health initiatives can be better designed to reduce malaria risk and improve health outcomes across different population groups.

Challenges, including data quality, ethical considerations, infrastructure limitations, and potential inequities, are critically examined.
AI-driven tools have demonstrated promising applications in several aspects of malaria control in Africa.
Ethical considerations also loom large in the adoption of AI for malaria control.
Capacity building represents another critical factor for suc cessful AI integration.

Annals of Medicine & Surgery (twenty twenty-five) eighty-seven:eight thousand, six hundred sixty-four–eight thousand, six hundred seventy Received twenty-one July twenty twenty-five; Accepted twenty-four October twenty twenty-five Published online thirty-one October twenty twenty-five.
Additional records were retrieved from the World Health Organization malaria database and reference lists of key articles.
Drone and mobile platforms improve vector mapping and real-time case reporting.
Genomic AI detects resistance mutations in Plasmodium.
Climate-informed models forecast transmission under environmental stress.
Ethical, infrastructural, and equity challenges require careful management.
These AI-pow ered systems can rapidly screen large numbers of samples, enabling faster diagnosis and treatment initiation.
Although still in early stages, such AI-based ecological and evolutionary simulations represent a powerful tool for anticipa tory malaria control.
These predictions enable proactive planning to avoid stockouts and ensure that essential commodities reach high-risk areas in a timely manner.
Data quality and bias AI systems rely on large, high-quality datasets for training and validation.
In many African contexts, health information systems are fragmented, and case reporting may be incom plete or inconsistent.
Inaccurate or biased input data can lead to erroneous predictions, misallocation of resources, and reinforcement of existing health disparities.
Ensuring rigor ous data cleaning, standardization, and representation across populations is therefore critical[three thousand, one hundred thirty-two].
Privacy and ethical concerns Malaria surveillance increasingly involves geospatial, geno mic, and personal health data.
Without robust governance, AI applications risk violating privacy, consent, and data sover eignty.
Many rural and underserved regions may lack these prerequisites, hindering adoption and sustainability.
Lack of transparency can erode trust, delay decision making, and complicate error correc tion.
Explainable AI approaches and stakeholder training are neces sary to enhance interpretability and account ability[three thousand, seven hundred thirty-eight].
Additionally, overreliance on externally developed AI solutions may undermine local ownership and capa city.
Prioritizing open-source platforms, local innovation, and inclusive implementation strategies can mitigate these risks[three thousand, nine hundred forty].
Without long-term planning, AI initia tives may become unsustainable once initial project funding ends.
Integrating AI into existing national malaria control fra meworks and securing multi-year support is essential for durable impact[twelve million, one hundred forty-four thousand, one hundred forty-two].
These AI-based systems generate seasonal transmission risk maps that guide the timing of IRS and community education campaigns.
Ensuring informed consent, confidentiality, and secure data storage is essential to maintain trust between communities and health authorities[forty-six].
Equitable access to AI-driven interventions is another critical concern.
Without deliberate planning, AI tools may preferentially benefit urban or better-resourced areas, exacerbating existing health disparities.
Transparency and accountability in AI decision making are also ethical imperatives.
By proac tively addressing privacy, equity, and transparency, AI can be deployed responsibly in African malaria programs.
Capacity building is another cornerstone for sustainable AI adoption.
AI models should be designed with explainability in mind, allowing users to comprehend how decisions are made and ensuring accountability[fifty-four].

This study assessed IHPs’ knowledgeofthediagnosis and treatment of malaria and diarrhea.
Methodology: A cross sectional quantitative study was conducted in eight urban informal settlements (slums) in southeast Nigeria.
Data were collected from informal health providers using an interviewer administered questionnaire.
Results: The mean overall knowledge scores for malaria and diarrhea were .
Respectively, among the different IHPs.
However, private medicine vendors (PMVs) and traditional birth attendants (TBAs) showed higher knowledge of treating malaria and diarrhea.
FrontiersinPublicHealth frontiersin.
Similarly, diarrhea is a leading cause of childhood mortality and morbidity in developing countries such as Nigeria.
There has been rapid urbanization in Nigeria, which has led to increases in risk factors for many communicable diseases.
This problem is compounded by weak healthcare systems that lack sufficient infrastructure to cope with these burdens (four).
Collaboration and partnerships with private sector actors, including both formal and informal healthcare providers, are essential (six).
They are often the first point of care for common childhood and adult illnesses for those living in urban informal settlements in Nigeria (eight).
Widely available IHPs present opportunities to improve access to appropriate essential health services in underserved urban areas in many LMICs (seven).
Several studies have highlighted the lack of understanding of malaria and diarrheal case management among informal providers (thirteen–fifteen).
Methods Study area The study was conducted in eight urban slums informal settlements, each in Enugu and Anambra states in southeastern Nigeria.
Enugu state had a population of approximately four.
Four million in twenty nineteen, while Anambra state had a population of five.
Six million in twenty nineteen with an estimated two.
Eighty-threepercent annual growth rate (one).
Administratively, Enugu and Anambra states have seventeen and twenty-one local government areas, respectively.
Urban dwellers in both states are mostly civil servants, traders, transporters, or artisans.
It was a quantitative cross-sectional study.
The study population was informal healthcare providers working in the purposively selected informal settlements.
Areas with security challenges were excluded from the study.
However, in their absence, any senior health provider in the facility was surveyed.
Pre-testing of the instrument was performed in two slums not included in the study to assess the clarity and simplicity of the questionnaire items.
The sample size was computed using the guidelines outlined in the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) listing manual (thirty-two).
Datafromformal health providers, however, were excluded from this study.

The findings on the availability of diagnostic equipment showed that the majority of IHPs lack basic equipment for providing care in their facilities.
Therefore, they rely mostly on patient history and symptoms to provide care.
The implications are that they may provide inaccurate diagnoses and delayed treatments, impacting the quality of care.
The findings on the method of diagnosis showed that the primary way informal providers diagnose malaria is by recognition of symptoms.
This is similar to the findings by Ayandipo et al.
(thirty-one) in Nigeria, where over eighty-five percent of health providers exhibited very poor malaria diagnostic practices.
This differs from the WHO case management protocol for malaria, which recommends microscopy, RDTs, or both for the diagnosis of malaria.
In this study conducted in Enugu and Anambra states in Nigeria, only a few IHPs diagnosed malaria using a rapid diagnostic test or microscopic examination of blood slides.
It implies that they either do not recognize the need or that they lack the competencies and equipment for correct diagnosis (nineteen).
Which ever is the case, improper diagnosis of malaria can lead to antimalarial drug resistance arising from inappropriate treatment.
Furthermore, antimalarial drug resistance could be a result of inappropriate treatment and the use of substandard drugs.
AMR is a global public health problem, with resistance to antibiotics causing an estimated one.
Three million deaths in twenty nineteen (twenty-two).
Training on the job, years of education, and the type of facility had a significant impact on knowledge regarding the treatment of malaria and diarrhea.
Furthermore,those who received on-the-job training, had more years of education, and worked as PMV or TBAs demonstrated better knowledge of treating malaria and diarrhea.
However, evidence shows that deploying training alone may have only a modest impact on performance (twenty-four).
These combined strategies have been found to be effective in improving the performance of IHPs (twenty-five).
Training and providing support has been found to be one of the ways of improving knowledge of diagnosis and treatment of any disease (twenty-six).
This would provide up-to-date knowledge of malaria and other common ailments.
This could facilitate improvements in the provision of quality health services by IHPs.
The use of only quantitative methodsis also alimitation as therecouldbebiasinthe respondent’s answer, and it cannot be used to infer certain factors.
However, the study has provided valuable information on informal health providers.
Informal health providers’ knowledge of the diagnosis and treatment of malaria and diarrhea is inadequate.
Providing quality education will, in turn, lead to improved quality of service delivery.

Between twenty twelve and twenty thirteen, IRS was piloted in two Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Nassarawa State, North-central Nigeria.
Uncertainties remain as to whether the intervention led to a decrease in the rate of malaria transmission or not.
Methodology: A simple SIRS model was used to generate a system of ordinary differential equations.
Results: The results showed a good fit of surveillance data to the numerical solutions of the model.
Over two years, IRS activities reduced the rate of malaria transmission in the intervention LGA by tenpercent.
The modest decrease was attributed to the way IRS was implemented and the uncertainties associated with using routine surveillance data in Nigeria.

[four] Indoor residual spraying (IRS) is the application of a long-lasting insecticide to mosquito-resting surfaces with a view to killing them.
[five] It is the second most common vector control strategy after long-lasting insecticidal nets.
When implemented correctly, IRS is highly effective, causing a rapid reduction in adult mosquito vector density and decreasing their lifespan.
[five] In the mid-ninetys, several malaria control programmes in Asia and America successfully used IRS to accelerate gains in malaria elimination.
[five] In Nigeria, several IRS interventions were conducted over the last two decades.
[eight–ten] Most of those interventions were small-scale pilot programmes that were implemented at the state level.
Major pilot activities took place in two thousand eight when the World Bank supported IRS activities in six states.
[ten] More campaigns were implemented in Lagos and Nassarawa States between twenty eleven and twenty thirteen.
[eight hundred twelve] Between twenty twelve and twenty thirteen, two IRS interventions were carried out in two Local Government Areas of Nassarawa State, North-central Nigeria.
[thirteen] These interventions were considered a success, having achieved lower densities of adult mosquitos in the two LGAs.
[fourteen] However, it is not clear if those interventions also led to a reduction in the rate of malaria transmission in the intervention areas or not.

Introduction Malaria continues to be the most important tropical infectious diseases, with high prevalence Globally.
Nigeria account for twenty-seven and thirty-onepercent of global cases and deaths, respectively [one], making malaria a significant public health burden in Nigeria.
The more recent localized National Malaria Indi cator survey (MIS) also tells the taletwo.
Malaria transmission across Africa exhibits significant heterogeneity owing to eco-climatic variations across the continent [three].
Currently, malaria infection in humans is attributed to five species of the Plasmodium parasites.
Primary vector species, such as Anopheles gambiae sensu lato (s.
[four], Anopheles funestus group, and Anopheles nili group [five–seven], primarily transmit the Plasmodium species causing human malaria in Africa.

Has been reported as a major malaria vector with the widest distribution and abundance [ten–twelve].
This limitation pres ents a significant challenge in the fight against malaria in Nigeria through vector control [ten].

Materials and methods Study area Nigeria (nine.
Six thousand, seven hundred fifty-three degree East) has thirty-six states plus FCT with an estimated population of twenty-one billion, five hundred twenty-six million, six hundred fifty-seven thousand, seven hundred twenty-eight.
Generally, the climate in the country is typically tropical with two distinct seasons, rainy (May to October) and dry (November to April).
The mean annual weather conditions in the country range from twenty-four.
Twenty degree celsius (Temperature), thirty-one.
One–eighty-fivepercent (Rela tive Humidity) and three hundred fourteen mm–eighteen seventy-one mm (Rainfall) [ten].
The main method of vector control in the study areas is insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs).

Hence, climatic and topographic level variables were used here to predict the distribution of the other Anopheline species (non-gambiae).
We considered nineteen environmental and four topographical variables as potential predictors of the target species habitat distribution [one hundred seventy-two thousand, three hundred twenty-four].
These variables were chosen based on their biological relevance to the target species distributions [twenty-five–twenty-eight].
The nineteen biocli matic variables with a two.
Five min spatial resolution (about. four percent).
One kmtwo) were downloaded from the WorldClim database (http://www.who.org.

The elevation data was used to generate slope, aspect, and hillshade (all in degrees) using the Spatial Analyst tool/surface in using ArcGIS ten.
After downloading the climatic files, the Nigeria layer was extracted by using a boundary mask.
Since some of these bioclimatic variables were strongly correlated (Rtwo greater than or equal to zero.
Seven), only those variables that demonstrated little correlation with other predictors were retained [ten].
Finally, a total of eleven environmental and topographical variables were selected in this study (Rtwo lesser than zero.
For the study area, the analysis requires both species presence and absence data and environmental variable (continuous or categorical) layers.
Before model construction, the predictor variables were standardized, using the scale function to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.

Discussion In Nigeria, significant progress has been made towards generating quality data for decision making.
This progress can be attributed to deployment of vector control tools alongside effec tive case management.
We also predicted distribution and relative abundance for the entire country using the random forest modeling approach.
About thirteen different non-gambiae species of Anopheles were encountered in this study, with most of them coexisting in sympatry at various locations.
These mosquitoes were found in ten out of the twenty states, spanning different ecological zones in the country.

Gambiae was found in all study locations, including states where non-gambiae species were not found.

Gambiae has been published elsewhere [ten].

Also, studies from other African countries have suggested that these species could exhibit higher vectorial capacity than the dominant vectors (Anopheles Gambiae).
Gambiae) and even maintain high malaria transmission during the dry season [three thousand, one hundred thirty-two].
Hence, understanding their distribution and spread in the country will help shape the focus of vector control in the country.

Ifeyinwa Arize *, Joy Ozughalu, Bernard Okechi , Chinyere Mbachu , Obinna Onwujekwe andBasseyEbenso ) Assessing .
This study assessed IHPs’ knowledgeofthediagnosis and treatment of malaria and diarrhea.
Methodology: A cross sectional quantitative study was conducted in eight urban informal settlements (slums) in southeast Nigeria.
Data were collected from informal health providers using an interviewer administered questionnaire.
Results: The mean overall knowledge scores for malaria and diarrhea were .
Respectively, among the different IHPs.
However, private medicine vendors (PMVs) and traditional birth attendants (TBAs) showed higher knowledge of treating malaria and diarrhea.
FrontiersinPublicHealth frontiersin.
Similarly, diarrhea is a leading cause of childhood mortality and morbidity in developing countries such as Nigeria.
There has been rapid urbanization in Nigeria, which has led to increases in risk factors for many communicable diseases.
This problem is compounded by weak healthcare systems that lack sufficient infrastructure to cope with these burdens (four).
Collaboration and partnerships with private sector actors, including both formal and informal healthcare providers, are essential (six).
They are often the first point of care for common childhood and adult illnesses for those living in urban informal settlements in Nigeria (eight).
Widely available IHPs present opportunities to improve access to appropriate essential health services in underserved urban areas in many LMICs (seven).
Several studies have highlighted the lack of understanding of malaria and diarrheal case management among informal providers (thirteen–fifteen).
Methods Study area The study was conducted in eight urban slums informal settlements, each in Enugu and Anambra states in southeastern Nigeria.
Enugu state had a population of approximately four.
Four million in twenty nineteen, while Anambra state had a population of five.
Six million in twenty nineteen with an estimated two.
Eighty-threepercent annual growth rate (one).
Administratively, Enugu and Anambra states have seventeen and twenty-one local government areas, respectively.
Urban dwellers in both states are mostly civil servants, traders, transporters, or artisans.
It was a quantitative cross-sectional study.
The study population was informal healthcare providers working in the purposively selected informal settlements.
Areas with security challenges were excluded from the study.
However, in their absence, any senior health provider in the facility was surveyed.
Pre-testing of the instrument was performed in two slums not included in the study to assess the clarity and simplicity of the questionnaire items.
The sample size was computed using the guidelines outlined in the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) listing manual (thirty-two).
Datafromformal health providers, however, were excluded from this study.

These statistics were presented as means and their associated ninety-fivepercent confidence intervals, as the questions had numerical responses.
The relationship between the knowledge score and respondents’ characteristics wasanalyzed.
Knowledge was summarized as composite scores, and two categories (adequate and inadequate knowledge) were generated.
These two categories of knowledge are supported by the literature (sixteen).
The scores were added up to create a knowledge ranking for the aforementioned categories.
The pooled scores of questions were classified into inadequate and adequate knowledge using median (fifty percent) scorevalues.
Inadequate knowledge was labeled as ‘one’, and adequate knowledge was labeled as ‘zero’.
All the respondents gave informed verbal consent and were assured of total anonymity.
