Despite the availability of interventions to prevent, diagnose and treat malaria, children under five years remain vulnerable.
Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC) is an effective intervention to prevent malaria in children under twenty-four months.
However, the uptake of PMC may be affected by community acceptability of the intervention.
The study explored the acceptability of PMC in Osun State, Nigeria.
Thematic analysis was conducted using ATLAS.
Results Participants reported acceptability of PMC delivered through expanded programme on immunization (EPI) platform.
On the other hand, lack of funds for transportation and the fear of side effects negatively affected PMC acceptability.
Caregivers reported the attitudes of health workers towards the intervention influenced their acceptance or negative behaviour towards PMC.
Religious leaders also accepted PMC as it did not contradict their faith.
Conclusion ARTICLE IN PRESS ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS Several factors affect acceptability of PMC.
In twenty twenty-three, sub-Saharan Africa accounted for over ninety-four percent (two hundred forty-six million) of malaria cases and ninety-five percent (five hundred sixty-nine thousand) of malaria-related deaths [one].
In Nigeria, malaria is the greatest cause of child mortality and an estimated ninety-five thousand children die from the disease each year [two].
The World Health Organization recommends several strategies for malaria prevention and control.
Intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi) has been shown to be safe and efficacious [four] [five] [six].
However, the effectiveness of PMC similar to other chemoprevention interventions is heavily dependent on its acceptability[nine] [ten].
Several factors such as acceptability ARTICLE IN PRESS could affect uptake of PMC [twelve].
Additional unscheduled pragmatic monthly doses are offered to children outside the EPI schedule up to eighteen months of age.
As part of a programme evaluation, a qualitative study was conducted to identify factors affecting acceptability of PMC.
Acceptability of malaria prevention interventions is shaped by multiple determinants.
Community knowledge and awareness of malaria and its preventive measures critically shape intervention acceptability.
Persistent misconceptions and limited understanding of the benefits of malaria prevention remain key barriers to acceptability and uptake [six hundred fourteen].
Gender dynamics further influence the acceptability of malaria prevention initiatives.
In many Nigerian communities, women have restricted autonomy in health-related decision-making [seventeen].
Health system efficiency and capacity also play a pivotal role in the implementation of preventive interventions.
This paper presents the findings of the qualitative component assessing acceptability of PMC implementation.
Across the eight LGAs, a total of forty intervention and forty control wards were identified for the study.
The LGAs included in the study are Ayedaade, Ede South, Atakunmosa West, Iwo, Irewole, Ife North, Obokun and Egbedore (Fig.
FGDs and KIIs were conducted in both PMC implementation areas (intervention arm) and non-PMC implementing areas (control arm).
Purposive sampling was employed to recruit participants with direct experience and involvement in the implementation of PMC intervention.
Their role is critical in studies on child health, nutrition, education, and behavioural sciences [eighteen nineteen].
Sampling technique and sample size determination The purposive sampling technique for this study comprised of four stages (Figure two).
At the first stage, all the eight LGAs selected for the implementation of PMC were included.
At the second stage, all the wards included in the implementation LGAs were grouped into either intervention ARTICLE IN PRESS or control wards.
Three wards each from intervention and control groups were randomly selected ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS for the qualitative study.
Each FGD comprised a minimum of six and maximum of twelve participants resulting in a total of one hundred fifty-six participants.
Only caregivers and fathers of children under twenty-four months whose children attend clinics at the sentinel health facilities selected were included.
Participation was voluntary and individuals who decline to participate were excluded.
For the FGDs for the caregivers, the participants were selected from caregivers who visit the sentinel facilities on the immunization days.
The KII and FGD guides for the community level were developed in English language and then FGD guides were translated to Yoruba, the local language.
Transcripts were translated back to English language.
Data collection Interview sessions were conducted at locations comfortable for the participants.
KIIs with health workers were conducted in English and FGDs with community members in Yoruba.
Each FGD and KII was moderated by a facilitator, supported by a note taker and audio recorded.
Each session lasted for an average of sixty minutes.
Voice recordings were uploaded to computers and correctly labelled each day.
Data analysis The data were analysed through a two-stage process.
The data collected were transcribed and translated into English.
Textual data were formatted as Microsoft Word files omitting name identifiers for confidentiality.
Data were then imported into Atlas-ti Version twenty-four software for analysis.
The qualitative data were analysed using ARTICLE IN PRESS thematic analysis.
Coding was conducted independently by two coders under the supervision of a Qualitative Analyst Expert to identify emerging themes.
Following initial coding, data were triangulated for internal validity to cross-check interpretation.
Participation in the study was voluntary, and participants had the right to withdraw at any stage of the study.
The informed consent forms were developed for the study and were read and interpreted (where applicable) to each participant.
Participants had the opportunity to ask questions about the study before giving their consent either by signature or thumb print on the form.
Anonymity and confidentiality of the participants were guaranteed.
Data were stored on a password-protected computer to prevent unauthorized access.
The age range of community leaders was thirty seventy-six years while that of health workers was thirty-five-fifty-eight years.
Health workers generally possessed a first degree.
Health workers’ years of experience ranged from ten to thirty-two years while the years spent in their current facility was between three and five years.
Thematic analysis Findings from this study revealed both facilitators and barriers to the acceptability of PMC.
Barriers that could affect PMC acceptability were also identified.
Several caregivers reported success stories, affirming that PMC was effective in ARTICLE IN PRESS preventing malaria among children.
On the benefit of PMC, caregivers expressed that PMC promotes health, vitality and prevents their children from falling ill.
Also, caregivers that are fathers agreed that PMC is good for their children because of their believe that it prevents malaria.
In addition, endorsement by health workers facilitated PMC acceptance.
“The malaria prevention… is very effective.
It prevents all sorts of illness”.
Prevention is better than cure.
They also would have thought about if it would affect a child or not.
Since they know it won't affect the child (negatively), we will collect it”.
For example, in Iwo, a community leader reported that their children were happy ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS when taking the drugs.
One caregiver explained that because the drugs are flavoured, children were more willing to take them.
“We discovered the children are happy… unlike injection that we force them to take”.
FGD with local leaders, Iwo.
One father reported that because the drugs are free, more people were motivated to take their children for PMC.
A health worker in Edunabon also confirmed that caregivers were happy to bring their children for PMC as the services they were providing were free.
“You know we are not collecting money for it, so they are happy about coming to be taking it”.
Also, caregivers in Iwo expressed trust in the health workers in administering both PMC and vaccine.
A caregiver in Edunabon explained that he did not support the use of herbs to treat illnesses but believes in the care provided at the hospital.
On the other hand, traditional medicine was refuted because it lacks information about the required measurement and the effectiveness of the herbs.
These statements imply that some community members already accepted conventional medicines as solution to health challenges for their families.
Community members who already trust and use conventional medicines are more likely to accept PMC.
Participants also expressed positive views on accepting PMC in their communities.
This was corroborated in a statement by a community leader in Edunabon that the drug was accepted because it prevents malaria.
This was further corroborated by a community leader in Iwo, who expressed that the rate of sicknesses in children has reduced.
Other factors include husbands’ refusal when the husbands do not accept routine immunization.
These findings mirror earlier research conducted in Mozambique and southern Tanzania, where similar community acceptance was reported [twenty-four twenty-five].
A key factor contributing to PMC acceptability was the formulation of the drug.
The use of flavoured, dispersible tablets enhanced both ease of administration by health workers and acceptance by caregivers.
This is consistent with earlier evidence that user-friendly formulations are critical for long-term programme sustainability [twenty-three].
Health worker counselling and interpersonal engagement also emerged as central facilitators of acceptability.
As shown in other community-based health interventions, active community engagement remains a cornerstone of success [twenty-six] [twenty-seven].
This finding aligns with prior evidence indicating that user fees can deter participation in preventive health programs [twenty-nine thirty].
Social relationships within health systems and communities also shaped PMC acceptability.
Positive interactions between health workers and caregivers, as previously reported in studies of IPTi [twenty-three], fostered trust and continuity of care.
The integration of PMC into the existing EPI platform appears to have further strengthened acceptance.
EPI services are widely trusted and routinely utilized, making them an ideal entry point for new interventions.
By utilizing a familiar and trusted delivery platform, PMC was perceived as a natural extension of routine child healthcare services.
Strengths and limitations The study has several strengths.
Methodological rigour was enriched using multiple qualitative data collection techniques, such as KIIs and FGDs.
However, the study has some limitations.
As with most qualitative studies, the findings are context-specific ARTICLE IN PRESS and may not be generalizable beyond similar settings.
In addition, interviews were conducted in local languages and nuances in meaning may have been lost during transcription and translation.
Acceptability of PMC reflects understanding of its benefits in reducing childhood malaria morbidity.
To maximize acceptance of PMC that would lead to increased uptake, identifying contextual factors that could influence acceptability is recommended.
We also appreciate the research assistants who provided technical support in the conduct of the study.
No funding bodies had any role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

Urban structure, also known as urban spatial structure (USS), illus- trates the structural patterns in cities and extended urban areas.
It is of note that within a city, the spatial structure landscape can vary dramat- ically from the Central Business District to the suburbs.
This is often as a result of dynamic economic structures with accompanied transforma- tion in the city’s socio-spatial organization [one].
Urban economists model USS based on the complex and interacting economic forces of decentral- ization, dispersion, and multiple employment [two].

Discussion The informal settlements are the core area or inner city.
They repre- sent the Central Business District, where the market, Obas palace, and earliest residential structures are located.
These places lack formal or modern form of urban planning.
Our study sup- ported this with distinct density characteristics between these settle-ments.
The medium-density settlements are often occupied by middle- class residents [fifteen, thirty-one].
The medium-density zone is followed by govern- ment residential estates earmarked for the affluent residents.
This zone is also regarded as the high-class residential areas [thirty-one, thirty-two].
The newly emerging areas are the peri-urban settle- ments found at the outskirts of the city.

Community education initiatives aim to raise awareness about malaria transmission, prevention, and treatment among at-risk populations.
BCC strategies are designed to promote positive health behav iors and reduce risky practices that contribute to malaria trans mission.
[seven] BCC employs a range of methods, including mass media campaigns, interpersonal communication, and social mobilization efforts.
These strategies are often tailored to spe cific cultural and social contexts to maximize their impact.
[eight] These interventions leverage local knowledge and resources, foster ing a sense of ownership and sustainability.
Despite their potential, the implementation of behavioral health interventions in malaria control faces several chal lenges.
[ten] Cultural beliefs and practices can influence the accep tance and effectiveness of these interventions.
Misconceptions about malaria transmission and treatment can hinder the adop tion of preventive measures and timely treatment-seeking behav ior.
[eleven] However, inadequate M&E frame works can limit the ability to measure outcomes and improve intervention strategies.
Community involvement is a critical factor in the success of behavioral health interventions.
Engaging communities in the design and implementation of interventions enhances their rele vance and acceptance.
[twelve] Community involvement fosters trust and ownership, leading to more sustainable and effective malaria control efforts.
Multi-sectoral collaboration is another important facilitator of effective behavioral health intervention.
Integrated approaches ensure that resources are efficiently utilized and efforts are synergistic.
For example, school-based education programs can be supported by health services to provide comprehensive malaria education and prevention.
These technologies pro vide scalable solutions for reaching wide audiences and facilitat ing real-time communication and feedback.
By leveraging these tools, malaria control programs can enhance the accessibility and effectiveness of their behavioral health interventions.
By doing so, the article intends to identify best practices and provide rec ommendations for future interventions and research in the field.
Studies and reports were selected based on their relevance to behavioral change strategies and their documented outcomes on malaria control.
Articles focused solely on clinical or pharmacological aspects of malaria with out behavioral components were excluded.
The implementation approaches, barriers, and enabling factors for each intervention were also analyzed to provide a holistic understanding.

Rationale Malaria remains a significant public health challenge, particu larly in sub-Saharan Africa and other tropical regions.
Behavioral health interventions, which include community education, behavior change communication, and the promotion of preventive practices (e.
Use of ITNs and IRS), are critical components of malaria control programs.
These interventions aim to modify individual and community behaviors to reduce malaria transmission and improve health outcomes.

Without adequate awareness and support, delays in treatment can lead to severe outcomes and continued community transmission.
These carri ers often fail to seek treatment, thereby sustaining the reservoir of infection within communities.
[three–five] In essence, a clear understanding of malaria pathogenesis underscores the importance of synchronizing prevention efforts with human behavior.
The success of antimalarial therapies, preventive tools, and vector control measures is profoundly influenced by individual and community behaviors.

[twenty] Behavior also influences the success of mass drug administration programs and community engagement initiatives.
[twenty-one] Ultimately, malaria is not merely a biological challenge but a social one.
Control efforts must extend beyond distributing commodities to understanding and addressing the human behaviors that determine their success.
The Role of behavioral health interventions in malaria control nine.
Community education Community education is a cornerstone of behavioral health interventions in malaria control.
[thirteen] It involves disseminating information and raising awareness about malaria transmission, prevention, and treatment among at-risk populations.
This approach leverages various channels, including schools, com munity centers, health clinics, and media platforms, to reach diverse audiences.
Objectives of community education The primary objectives of community education in malaria con trol are to: one.
Promote preventive measures: Encourage the consistent use of ITNs, IRS, and other preventive measures.
Improve treatment-seeking behavior: Motivate individ uals to seek prompt and appropriate medical treatment when malaria symptoms appear.
Foster community involvement: Engage community mem bers in malaria control activities to build local capacity and sustain efforts.
Methods of community education one.
School-based programs: Schools provide an effective plat form for educating children and, by extension, their fam ilies.
Programs may include classroom lessons, interactive activities, and distribution of educational materials.
Community health talks: Health talks conducted at com munity centers, marketplaces, and religious gatherings can reach large audiences.
These sessions often involve local health workers or volunteers who provide informa tion and answer questions about malaria.
Media campaigns: Mass media campaigns utilize radio, television, newspapers, and social media to disseminate information widely.
These campaigns can reach a broad audience and reinforce key messages through repetition.
These sessions often include practical demonstra tions on the use of ITNs and other preventive measures.
[fourteen] For instance, a study in rural Kenya found that educational campaigns increased ITN usage from thirty percent to seventy percent over three years.
Community engagement: Involving local leaders and com munity members in planning and delivering education activities fosters ownership and trust.
Sustainability: Ensuring that education efforts are continu ous and supported by local resources and capacity-building initiatives.
Challenges in implementation one.
Cultural barriers: Misconceptions about malaria trans mission and treatment can hinder the effectiveness of edu cation efforts.
Some communities may have traditional beliefs that conflict with modern medical advice.
Resource constraints: Limited funding, personnel, and materials can restrict the reach and frequency of educa tional activities.
Access issues: In remote or conflict-affected areas, reach ing target populations with educational messages can be challenging.
Medicine (twenty twenty-five) one hundred four:thirty-one www.who.org
Strategies for overcoming challenges one.
Objectives of BCC in malaria control The primary objectives of BCC in malaria control are to: one.
Increase knowledge: Enhance understanding of malaria transmission, symptoms, prevention, and treatment among target populations.
Promote preventive behaviors: Encourage the consistent use of ITNs, IRS, and other preventive measures.
Improve treatment-seeking behavior: Motivate individu als to seek prompt and appropriate medical care at the f irst signs of malaria symptoms.
Reduce risky practices: Discourage behaviors that increase the risk of malaria, such as improper use of ITNs and delayed treatment-seeking.
Mass media campaigns: Utilizing radio, television, news papers, and social media to disseminate information widely.
These campaigns can reach broad audiences and reinforce key messages through repeated exposure.
Interpersonal communication: Engaging individuals and small groups in direct conversations about malaria pre vention and treatment.
This method includes counseling sessions, peer education, and community dialogs.
Community mobilization: Involving community members and leaders in malaria control activities to foster collec tive action and ownership.
This can include organizing community meetings, health fairs, and participatory workshops.
These methods can effectively capture attention and promote behavior change.
Print and digital materials: Distributing brochures, posters, and leaflets in public places, health facilities, and homes.
Efficacy of BCC BCC has been shown to be effective in changing behaviors and reducing malaria transmission.
[twenty-one] Ensuring that messages and delivery methods are culturally appropriate and resonate with the target audience.
This includes using local languages, idioms, and culturally significant symbols.
Repeated exposure to key messages through multiple channels reinforces learning and encourages behavior change.
Creating opportunities for dialogue and feedback to address concerns, misconceptions, and barriers to behavior change.
Continuously assessing the impact of BCC activities to refine strategies and improve effectiveness.
This involves collecting data on behavior changes and health out comes, and adjusting campaigns based on findings.
Deep-rooted beliefs and practices can be resistant to change.
Misconceptions about malaria transmission and treatment can undermine BCC efforts.
[twenty-two] Insufficient funding, trained personnel, and materials can limit the scope and reach of BCC campaigns.
Reaching remote or conflict-affected areas with BCC messages can be challenging.
Overexposure to health messages can lead to desensitization and reduced impact.
Engaging community leaders and members in the design and delivery of BCC activities ensures cultural relevance and increases acceptance.
[twenty-three] Collaborating with nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), government agencies, and local institutions can enhance resources and exper tise.
Medicine (twenty twenty-five) one hundred four:thirty-one Medicine implementation, and evaluation of malaria prevention and treatment strategies.
Establishing robust monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems to track progress, identify challenges, and inform programmatic adjustments.
Objectives of community-based interventions The primary objectives of community-based interventions in malaria control are to: one.
Empower communities: Build local capacity and leader ship to take ownership of malaria control activities.
Promote participation: Engage community members in identifying needs, setting priorities, and implementing solutions.
Improve access to services: Increase access to malaria pre vention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the commu nity level.
Strengthen social support: Foster supportive environ ments that encourage adherence to preventive measures and treatment protocols.
Methods of community-based interventions one.
These bar riers can undermine even the most evidence-based strategies if not adequately addressed.
This section outlines key obstacles to implementation and highlights adaptive strategies that have shown promise in overcoming them.
Resistance to IRS and distrust of ITNs may stem from fears of infertility, toxicity, or political suspicion.
Culturally sensi tive engagement is critical.
Involving respected local leaders, traditional healers, and religious figures in health education efforts enhances trust and message legitimacy.
Tailoring mes sages in local languages and using storytelling, drama, or oral traditions can improve message retention and acceptance.
Printed materials may be ineffective in pop ulations with limited reading proficiency.
CHWs trained in participatory communication techniques can foster dialogue and clarify misconceptions.
Socio-economic constraints Poverty often limits access to preventive tools and health ser vices.
Even when ITNs are distributed for free, the indirect costs of care (e.
Transportation, time off work, or clinic fees) dis courage treatment-seeking behavior.
Behavioral interventions must be paired with social support mechanisms.
Conditional cash transfers, transportation vouchers, and community-based health insurance schemes can help remove financial barriers.
Moreover, aligning malaria interventions with broader poverty reduction efforts increases sustainability and equity.
Capacity-building initia tives, such as training CHWs in BCC, can decentralize service delivery and increase community reach.
Digital tools like mobile reporting systems or SMS-based health tips can enhance effi ciency and monitoring.
Inconsistent program funding and political support Donor-dependent programs often suffer from discontinuity when funding cycles end.
A lack of political commitment can further undermine behavioral health investments.

Com for domestic resource mobilization and integrating behavioral health into national malaria control strategies can enhance pro gram sustainability.
Multi-sectoral collaboration – including education, housing, and agriculture – ensures broader buy-in and resource pooling.
Monitoring and evaluation challenges Behavioral outcomes are inherently complex and often slow to manifest.
Poorly designed evaluation frameworks may fail to capture nuanced changes in attitudes, beliefs, or long-term behaviors.
[five thousand, three hundred fifty-four] Mixed-methods approaches that combine quan titative indicators (e.
ITN usage rates) with qualitative tools (e.
Focus group discussions, community feedback) offer a more comprehensive evaluation of behavioral interventions.
Community-led monitoring models can also enhance account ability and local ownership.
Community-based interventions harness the power of local communities in driving malaria control activ ities.

The capital of Nasarawa State is Lafia, which serves as an administrative and commercial hub for the region [thirty-one].
Lafia is strategically located within the state, lying at longitude eight degree East, and latitude eight degree North (Fig.
This city has experienced significant growth in recent years, driven by its role as a center for trade and commerce.
The urbanization of Lafia has attracted a mix of people from various backgrounds, con tributing to its cultural diversity.
The region experiences two primary seasons: a wet season and a dry season.
The wet season typically occurs from April to October, characterized by well-distributed rain fall and a monthly mean of about one hundred forty-five.
Twenty-three mm, culminat ing in an annual average of approximately eleven sixty-one.
The peak rainfall occurs in July and August, contributing to the lush vegetation that defines the landscape during this period.
Conversely, the dry season spans from November to March, marked by significantly reduced rainfall.

The choice of a community-based approach allowed for an in-depth understanding of the health dynamics within the popu lation.
Data collection was conducted using structured ques tionnaires and clinical assessments, which were admin istered by trained field researchers.
This partnership facilitated access to local resources and networks, enhancing the overall efficacy of the data col lection process.
Ethical clearance Ethical clearance for this study was obtained through the Otunsha Foundation from the State’s Ministry of Health.
Semi-structured questionnaires were administered after explaining the details of the study and procedure.
These criteria served as guidelines for iden tifying individuals who were eligible to participate in the research.
Inclusion Criteria included individuals residing within the Lafia East section of Lafia Local Government Area.
Addition ally, individuals who had been diagnosed with malaria or hepatitis B and C viruses at any point prior to the study Aremu et al.
Furthermore, participants who were willing to pro vide informed consent and actively engage in the study were also eligible.
Exclusion Criteria comprised several factors to main tain the integrity of the study.
Preg nant or breastfeeding women were also excluded from participation to minimize potential risks to both mater nal and child health.

The study population consisted of two hundred sixty-four participants (two hundred sixty-four), drawn from the Lafia community in Nasarawa State, Nigeria.
These individuals included male and female patients of various ages, encompassing both adults and children.
A total of two hundred sixty-four questionnaires were administered to adults seeking testing.
The study was conducted over a six-month period from April to Octo ber twenty twenty-four.
All tests were performed in accordance with standard procedures and practices following the manu facturer’s instructions.
The blood samples were transferred into an ethylenedi aminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tube to prevent coagula tion.
Two blood films were prepared from each sample: one thin and one thick.
The thick and thin smears were made on clean, dry microscope glass slides and allowed to air-dry.
The stained slides were examined under a microscope using oil immersion at one hundredx magnification.
Parasite density was quantified against two hundred leukocytes, based on an assumed leukocyte count of eight thousand cells/µl of blood [thirty-two].
The degree of parasite density was graded as mild ( lesser than one thousand parasites/µl), moderate (one thousand–nine thousand, nine hundred ninety-nine Aremu et al.
The calculation for parasites per µl of blood was as follows: Parasites/ul of blood equal to No.
Of asexual stages × eight thousand leu kocytes/two hundred leukocytes.
The malaria test procedure was carried out using the CareStart kit.
The strip from the sealed foil pouch was gently removed, and the sample number was recorded on the strip and the cassette.
Following this, five µl of whole blood was added into the “S” well, along with sixty µl of assay buffer.
The result was read after twenty min and documented.
This means that one band appears in the control area, and another band appears in the test area.
This result suggests that the individual has tested positive for the specific disease being tested (malaria, HBsAg, or HCV).
Negative Result: If only one band is visible, located in the control area, this indicates a negative result.
In this case, the absence of a band in the test area suggests that the individual does not have the disease being tested for.
Invalid Test: The test result is considered invalid if the control band does not appear at all.
This situation indicates a potential error in the test procedure, such as improper handling or a malfunction of the test kit.
In such cases, the test should be repeated to ensure accurate results.
These tests offer a quick and efficient way to diag nose infections, enabling timely medical intervention.
Prior to the punc ture, the area was cleaned using an alcohol swab to minimize the risk of contamination.
Following this, a drop of buffer solution was added to facilitate the test ing process.
The results were read at fifteen min, in accor dance with the manufacturer’s instructions [thirty-two].
These rapid test strips exhibit high accuracy, with a sen sitivity of ninety-nine.
The sample number was recorded on the strip for identification purposes.
The result was evaluated after fifteen min, allowing sufficient time for the red line to develop.
Negative Result: The presence of only one band in the control area signifies a negative result.
Test procedure for Hepatitis C virus testing Similarly, the procedure for testing for hepatitis C virus (HCV) followed the same initial steps.
After removing the strip from the sealed foil pouch, the sample number was written on the strip.
Two drops of whole blood were added into the “sample pad” of the test strip, and one drop of buffer was subsequently added.
The results were read after ten min, as this timeframe is optimal for the development of the red line.
Positive Result: A positive result for hepatitis C is indicated by two color bands: one in the control area and another in the test area.
Invalid Test: As with the HBsAg test, if the control band does not appear, the test is considered invalid, and retesting is recommended.
Age was recorded to capture the age distri bution of respondents, while sex differentiated between male and female participants.
Family size was assessed to understand household dynamics and potential influences on health and resource allocation.
The source of water was included to evaluate the quality of water supply, crucial for under standing exposure to waterborne diseases.
Questions regarding prophylaxis aimed to gather information about the use of preventive treatments for diseases.
The use of insecticides was explored to understand exposure to vec tor control measures, particularly relevant for diseases such as malaria.
Information on tribal marks or tattoos was included to examine cultural practices that might relate to health beliefs and behaviors.
Blood transfusion history was documented to evaluate any previous trans fusions that might be relevant for screening blood-borne infections.

The results revealed no significant differences in the prevalence of these con ditions based on sex.
Marital status appeared to play a more pronounced role, particularly in the prevalence of malaria and HCV.
Single individuals demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence of malaria compared to married individuals.
This difference could reflect variations in living condi tions, exposure risks, or access to preventive measures, as Aremu et al.
Interestingly, income level did not significantly influ ence the prevalence of any of the three conditions.
Both low-income and middle-income individuals exhibited comparable rates of malaria, HBsAg, and HCV [thirty-two].
This f inding suggests that in this context, socioeconomic dis parities may not play a decisive role in determining expo sure or susceptibility.
This uniformity underscores the need for widespread, community-based interventions rather than income-targeted programs.
Age emerged as a critical factor, particularly in the prevalence of malaria and HCV.
Notably, no HCV cases were reported among individuals aged nine–seventeen, high lighting a potential age-related variation in exposure or vulnerability [one hundred].
Despite these differences for malaria and HCV, the prevalence of HBsAg did not vary signifi cantly across age groups.
The findings of this study have important implications for public health strategies.
For HCV, the significant differences observed by marital status and age warrant further investigation into underly ing transmission dynamics.
T he socioeconomic landscape of the study population revealed a predominance of low-income individuals, with eighty-eight.
Six percent categorized as low-income.
This finding reflects a common trend in malaria-endemic regions where poverty exacerbates the risk of infection [thirty-two].
The use of borehole water as the primary water source among participants (eighty-nine.
Four percent) may raise concerns about the quality of water and its implications for health.
Clinical manifesta tions often prompt individuals to seek medical atten tion, leading to diagnosis and subsequent management of infections.
Overall, this study underscores the diverse factors influencing the prevalence of malaria, HBsAg, and HCV in Lafia, Nasarawa State.
It highlights the need for tai lored public health strategies that address the unique vul nerabilities of different population groups.
Public education campaigns should encourage consistent net usage and active community participation in vector control ini tiatives.
Equally important is the enhancement of vac cination programs targeting hepatitis [two–three, twenty-one–twenty-three, thirty].
Health authorities must focus on increasing awareness of and accessibility to hepatitis vaccinations, particularly among high-risk populations.
Improving water quality and access in the town is another crucial step.
Such integrated programs should pri oritize screening and treatment to deliver holistic care [thirty-two].
This will enable the design of evi dence-based interventions.
Lastly, policy advocacy must address the socioeconomic determinants of health, such as poverty and low health literacy.
Through poverty alle viation, education, and health literacy programs, public health efforts can achieve sustainable improvements [thirty-two].
Limitations of the study A significant limitation of this study is its cross-sectional design, which captures data at a single point in time.
This approach, while useful for estimating prevalence, does not provide insights into temporal trends or causative relationships between variables.
The study’s geographic focus is another constraint, as it is limited to a specific popula tion in Lafia, Nasarawa State, Nigeria.
Including these variables could have enriched the analysis and offered more actionable insights.
Despite standard diagnostic techniques being used, potential diagnostic inaccuracies remain a limitation.
The study also did not explore the genetic variability of the pathogens, which can significantly affect disease prevalence and severity.
Future research incorporat ing a longitudinal design could provide a more dynamic understanding of disease patterns and their drivers.
Overall, while the study offers valuable prevalence data, it highlights the need for further research to address these limitations.
This complex interplay between malaria, HBsAg, and HCV emphasizes the urgent need for an integrated public health approach.
A multi faceted approach is necessary to effectively reduce the prevalence of malaria and viral hepatitis, particularly in low-income populations.
Addressing these interconnected health challenges will contribute to a healthier, more resilient community.

In our experience, researchers often face challenges in engaging non-technical stake holders in data analysis and interpretation.
Nevertheless, this should be seen not as a limitation of the process, but as a lesson learned.
One key driver for developing this framework was the time constraints surrounding the decision-making process.
Given the heavy workload that malaria program staff often experience, this is likely a common feature of their work.
We are currently conducting trainings to facilitate the adoption of the tool during future planning for bed net distribution in urban areas.
The limitations of this work fall into three categories: those related to the study’s conduct, the frame work’s structure, and its application.
These limitations should be addressed in future efforts to refine the framework.
Observations from Ilorin revealed that unclear community boundaries, despite microplanning, created confusion during bed net distribution.
However, publicly available satellite imagery often lacks the resolution required for such mapping and may not be up to date.
Additionally, malaria programs frequently lack the resources and capacity to acquire and process real-time, high-resolution imagery.
Overcoming these two challenges would represent a significant advancement not only for malaria programs but also for other health initiatives.
Future applications of this framework must carefully consider the decision-making process for excluding areas from intervention campaigns.
In settings with severe funding constraints, larger areas, including informal settlements and slums, may need to be deprioritized.
Addressing this gap should be a priority in future work.

Nigeria is the single largest con tributor to the burden in Africa and globally [two].
In twenty twenty-two, the country recorded an estimated sixty-eight.
One million cases and one hundred eighty-nine thousand, three hundred deaths from malaria, which accounted for forty-four.
Zero percent of deaths from the twelve ‘high-burden, high-impact’ (HBHI) countries [three].
However, several critical questions must be addressed to optimise pre-referral treatment strategies in Nige ria.
The Children Specialist Hos pital, a healthcare facility with thirty-five beds, is strategically Ibrahim et al.
Malaria Journal Page three of nine positioned in the central district of Ilorin.
This ancient city serves as the capital of Kwara State, one of the six states that constitute Nigeria’s north–central region.
It is the only government-owned dedicated paediatric hos pital within the state with an estimated population size of three million, five hundred fifty-one thousand (twenty twenty-two).
The hospital is supported by free malaria diagnostics and treatments from the Kwara State Ministry of Health and its partners.
Sample size estimation T he minimum sample estimate was calculated using an online sample size calculator (http:// www.html)
At ninety-five percent confidence and a five percent margin of error.
Using prevalence of severe malaria (eighteen.
However, the final data analysis included all one hundred thirty-seven children with severe malaria who were admitted during the study period.
Patient recruitment and management Consecutive children who met the inclusion criteria were recruited from July one, twenty twenty-three, to August thirty-one, twenty twenty-four.
Children with severe anaemia received blood transfusion.
Patients were discharged from the hospital following clinical improvement for subsequent follow-up care.
Also, additional calls were made to the refer ring facility to confirm the administration of medications prior to referrals where indicated.
The study protocol was administered by a trained research assistant and super vised by the consultant paediatrician (a member of the research team).
Data analysis T he obtained data were entered into an Excel spread sheet and updated regularly.
After data cleaning, the data were transferred and analysed using IBM-SPSS version twenty-nine.
The age distribution of the children was not normally distributed and was summarised using the median and interquartile range.
Malaria Journal and further compared using Fischer’s exact test.
The level of statistical significance was set at p lesser than zero.
Ethical consideration and approval This study was approved by the Kwara State Ministry of Health Ethics Review Committee.
This study was con ducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Informed consent was obtained from the parents and guardians of all participating children.
Data were main tained with strict confidentiality, secured in a password protected computer, and de-identified during the analysis process.

Setting The study was conducted at the immunisation clinic of a tertiary health centre in Northcentral Nigeria.
Participants A total of three hundred seventy-six women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years) participated in the study.
All participants resided in the study area and had children aged zero–five years.
Results Awareness of the malaria vaccine was low, with only eighty-nine mothers (twenty-three.
Seven percent) reporting prior knowledge of it.
Despite this, an overwhelming three hundred sixty-six participants (ninety-seven.
Three percent) expressed willingness to vaccinate their children and three hundred fifty-two (ninety-three.
Six percent) were willing to pay for the vaccine.
Concerns about injection site reactions, fever and pain were common, with one hundred twenty-six mothers (thirty-three.
Six percent) preferring an oral vaccine.
Positive perception significantly influenced willingness to vaccinate (X² equal tofive.
Additionally, age, marital status, educational level and income were significantly associated with willingness to vaccinate (p equal tozero.
At the multivariate level, younger maternal age (OR equal toone.
Eleven) and higher income (OR equal toone.
Forty-nine) emerged as direct predictors of vaccine acceptance.
The findings highlight the importance of targeted educational campaigns to improve awareness and acceptance of malaria vaccines.
Future studies should explore interventions to enhance vaccine acceptance and address potential barriers to vaccine awareness.

A large sample size enhances the reliability of findings within the study population.

Those who were seriously ill and unable to respond were excluded from the study.
Four percent positive perception of the malaria vaccine, based on a study by Chukwuocha et alnineteen in Southeastern Nigeria.
This calculation initially resulted in three hundred sixty-four participants.
Including a ten percent non- response rate, the final sample size was set at three hundred seventy-six.
The sample frame was the attendance register of the immunisation clinic of the study location while the sampling interval (K) was three.
Data collec tion was conducted on clinic days (Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays) averaging twenty-one respondents per day and sixty-three respondents per week.
Each third mother on the atten dance register on each clinic day was randomised (K equal tothree).
Twenty–twenty-two It had four sections: socio demographic data, awareness of the malaria vaccine, perceptions of the vaccine and willingness to accept it.
Awareness was eval uated by asking if they had heard of the vaccine, with ‘yes’ scored as one and ‘no’ as zero.
The study also explored sources of awareness and barriers to vaccine acceptance.
Research assistants ensured all questions were answered.
Data analysis Data analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS V.
Twenty-seven, describing categorical variables with frequencies and percentages.
Χtwo tests and multivariate binary logistic regression were used, with significance set at p lesser than zero.
Prevalence rates for awareness, perception and willingness to accept the malaria vaccine were calculated.
The main outcome variable, willingness to vaccinate children under age five, was cross-tabulated with sociodemographic characteristics.
Five in binary logistic anal ysis were included in the multivariate model, with results presented as adjusted ORs and ninety-five percent CIs.
The research questions were developed based on the challenges faced in the implementation of new vaccines in the past.

Fear of injection site reactions, fever and pain was a notable concern among respondents, with thirty-three.
Six percent prefer ring a non- injectable vaccine.
This preference aligns with findings from other studies.
Oduwole et althirty-five noted that less invasive vaccine delivery methods, such as oral vaccines, improved acceptance in Kenya and Tanzania.
Goldstein et althirty-seven demonstrated that tailored educational interventions effectively reduced vaccine hesitancy.
Enhancing surveillance and reporting systems for adverse events following immuni sation is also vital.
Transparent reporting and prompt management of adverse events can build public trust, as emphasised by the WHO’s Global Vaccine Safety Initiative.
This underscores the importance of shaping perceptions, not just spreading information.
Brewerforty also identified positive beliefs about vaccine efficacy and safety as key predictors of vaccination rates.
Educational campaigns should focus on addressing common fears and misconceptions to foster a positive perception of the malaria vaccine.
Kara fillakis and Larsonforty-one found that targeted communication addressing vaccine safety concerns significantly improved acceptance.
Engaging trusted community figures and using storytelling can enhance these efforts.
For instance, Jegedeforty-two demonstrated that involving religious and traditional leaders in vaccination campaigns in Nigeria increased uptake.
Personal testimonials from parents with positive vaccination experiences, as highlighted by Betsch et al,forty-three can also effectively shift perceptions.
The study identified several factors influencing vaccine acceptance, including positive perception, maternal age and income.
Younger caregivers and those with higher incomes were more likely to accept the vaccine, consis tent with findings by Adedini et altwenty-four and Musa et al.

Positive perceptions of vaccine safety and efficacy were key predictors of uptake, as shown by Betsch et al.
Forty-three Tailored educational interven tions are necessary to build trust and address concerns.
Jarrett et alforty-four demonstrated the effectiveness of tailored communication strategies in improving vaccine uptake.
Understanding maternal age and income can help target interventions more effectively.
Merten et alforty-five found social media to be an effective tool for health communi cation among younger demographics.
Financial barriers can be addressed by offering vaccines at subsidised rates or integrating them into free immunisation programmes.
Bednarczyk and Birkheadforty-six showed that reducing finan cial barriers increased vaccine uptake among low- income populations.
Maternal education also plays a significant role in vaccine acceptance.
Educated mothers are more likely to understand the benefits of vaccination and actively seek it for their children.
Abdulraheem et alforty-seven found a positive correlation between maternal educa tion levels and vaccination rates.
Educational campaigns targeting less educated mothers, providing them with necessary information and support, can help bridge this gap.
Socioeconomic factors such as income and maternal education should inform public health policies to ensure equitable access to malaria vaccines.
CONCLUSIONS The study found a low awareness of the malaria vaccine among the study population.
However, there was a posi tive perception towards the vaccine.
There was a high level of willingness to accept the malaria vaccine.
Factors affecting willingness include age, socioeconomic status and positive perception.
These strategies will help improve acceptance of the malaria vaccine and are crucial for reducing malaria’s burden.
Future research should assess the effectiveness of these interventions and explore additional factors affecting vaccine acceptance.
Health workers should include malaria vaccine educa tion as part of their health education sessions.

This is an increase of eleven million cases above twenty twenty-two global estimates and a rise in incidence from fifty-eight.

Despite growing recognition of malaria’s neurologi cal impact, the true burden of stroke in malaria-endemic regions remains underreported.
This diagnos tic ambiguity often results in misclassification, which delays appropriate interventions and leads to worse clinical out comes [seven].
Addressing this knowledge gap can inform public health strategies that integrate stroke prevention and management into malaria-endemic settings.
This paper examines the incidence, clinical presentation, and outcomes of stroke in malaria.
Gray literature was identified through Google Scholar, WHO Malaria Reports, and regional stroke regis tries (e.
African Stroke Organization).
To minimize selection bias, manual searches of reference lists from relevant articles, systematic reviews, and meta analyses were performed.
Duplicate records were removed using EndNote (version Xnine).
Study focus: Reported data on stroke incidence, clinical features, risk factors, or outcomes in malaria patients.
Study design: Original peer-reviewed studies (e.
Case reports, case series, cohort studies, cross-sec tional studies).
Outcome measures: Reported at least one of stroke incidence, subtype (ischaemic vs.
Haemorrhagic), neurological deficits, mortality, or long-term disabil ity.
Language: English-language publications.
Exclusion criteria included: Studies on animal models or in vitro research.
Non-peer-reviewed articles (editorials, conference abstracts).
Studies lacking stroke-specific data or confirmation of malaria.

Results This review includes a total of nine studies [eight–sixteen] pub lished between nineteen ninety-nine and twenty twenty-four.
The studies consisted of case reports and case series, with ages ranging from two to forty-seven years (Table two).
The treatment protocols across the studies were largely con sistent, with anti-malarial therapy as the cornerstone.
Support ive care, including fluid management and antipyretics, was also widely implemented.
Malaria species Plasmodium falciparum was frequently associated with hemorrhagic strokes [eight–ten].
The severity of these complications highlights the heightened risk of stroke in individuals infected with P. falciparum.
Age and demographics The age range of patients affected by stroke due to malaria spans a wide spectrum.
Regarding gender, no clear predomi nance was observed in the studies reviewed.
However, the sample sizes were generally small, which limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions about gender-spe cific risks and trends.
Hemiparesis or hemiplegia was observed in several cases [eight, fourteen, fifteen].
Stroke types Malaria-related strokes predominantly include two types: ischaemic and haemorrhagic strokes.
On the other hand, haem orrhagic strokes were more commonly associated with P.falciparum.
Falciparum infections, with cerebral parenchymal haem orrhage [eight] and venous infarcts due to thrombosis [fifteen] frequently reported.
The MCA was the most frequently reported territory, potentially due to mechani cal obstruction by parasitized red blood cells (RBCs).
Vivax malaria Acute cerebral infarct in P.falciparum.
Malaria Journal Page six of nine with falciparum malaria, but specific venous territories (e.
Superior sagittal sinus, transverse sinus) were not detailed.
Clinical presentations included focal neurologi cal deficits and altered consciousness, consistent with CVT’s typical manifestations.
Diagnostic challenges Misdiagnosis remains a significant challenge in the man agement of malaria-related strokes.
Several cases were initially misdiagnosed or not considered for stroke, lead ing to delayed interventions.
The aggregation of parasitized red blood cells in small vessels can lead to local ischaemia, thereby exacerbating neurological deficits.
Prompt initiation of anti-malarial therapy is crucial in reducing parasitaemia and preventing further brain vascular damage.
In addition to anti-malarial therapy, supportive care is a crucial component in managing these complex cases.
This includes the administration of antibiotics to treat potential secondary infections, which are common in patients with severe malaria [ten].
Many patients demonstrated significant neurological improvement with timely and appropriate treatment.
Early recognition and man agement of stroke symptoms were key factors contribut ing to better recovery.
However, mortality rates were notably high in cases with severe complications, particularly those involving cerebral venous thrombosis.
Discussion T his review synthesized the current evidence on the incidence, clinical presentation, and outcomes of stroke in patients with malaria.
This is particularly important in paediatric populations, where neurological complications of malaria are often underreported [twenty].
A significant takeaway from this review is the recur ring issue of delayed diagnosis or misdiagnosis of stroke in malaria patients.
The poten tial for misdiagnosis highlights the need for improved diagnostic protocols and a more systematic approach to patient evaluation.
Malaria exacerbates pre-existing vascular vulnerabilities, such as endothe lial dysfunction, which predispose specific individuals to stroke [twenty-one].
The pathophysiology of stroke in malaria is complex and multifactorial.
Given the role of endothelial damage and thrombosis in ischaemic stroke, antiplatelet therapy could mitigate these effects.
This suggests that stroke in malaria is not simply a mechani cal phenomenon but also a consequence of the body’s immune response to the infection.
This finding calls for a more Aderinto et al.
Malaria Journal Page eight of nine holistic understanding of how malaria interacts with host biology to produce neurological damage.
T he management of stroke in malaria patients involves a combination of anti-malarial therapy, symp tomatic management, and supportive care.
However, there is limited evidence on how effec tively these therapies specifically address stroke-related pathology.
Anti-malarial treatment should be administered as early as possible to reduce the parasite burden and prevent further vascular damage.
However, this must be complemented by targeted neuroprotective thera pies, particularly in patients with severe neurological complications.
The management of stroke in the context of malaria also highlights the impor tance of timely intervention.
Several gaps exist in the current understanding of malaria-related stroke, warranting further investiga tion.
Moreover, more research is needed to understand the relative con tributions of different Plasmodium species to stroke risk.
However, this review has some limitations.
Stroke, both ischaemic and haem orrhagic, is a serious complication of malaria, with P.
Fal ciparum more frequently associated with haemorrhagic strokes, and P. vivax contributing to ischemic events.

Methods A systematic search of Medline (PubMed), Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and other manually searched articles yielded five hundred two records.
After removing duplicates and screening, fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.
The risk of bias and applicability were assessed via QUADAS-two.
Four and the metafor package (version four.
Six–zero) in R (version four.
Publication bias was assessed via funnel plots and Egger’s test.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of pooled estimates.
Results The pooled sensitivity of RDTs was sixty-nine.
Seven percent [ninety-five percent confidence interval (CI)]: sixty-seven.
Six percent, and the specificity was eighty-one.
The SROC curve was zero.
Nine hundred two, though heterogeneity was high (Itwo  equals to ninety-six.
Subgroup analysis showed regional variability, with better performance in urban settings.
Funnel plot asymmetry and Egger’s test suggested publication bias.
Leave-one-out analyses confirmed robustness, with pooled estimates ranging sixty-eight–seventy-five percent for sensitivity, eighty-eight–ninety-one percent for specificity, and seventeen.
Conclusion Malaria RDTs in Nigeria show suboptimal sensitivity and specificity compared with WHO benchmarks.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimates, reinforcing the validity of the conclusions.
